items.body: Across a discography that ranges from politically charged works such as Palestine Is Always War and In the Life of a Palestinian Prisoner to the nostalgic reimagining of Arabic popular song found on Orientalism, Bouncyduck has consistently refused to be defined by a single mood or aesthetic. His music moves freely between social commentary, cultural memory, humour and personal reflection. It’s Either Me or My Auntie perhaps brings these different strands together most successfully, transforming a beloved Egyptian comedy into a surprisingly moving and deeply life-affirming electronic album. Built from fragments of the film starring Mohamed Henedi, the record turns familiar dialogue into hypnotic techno constructions where humour, memory and repetition become inseparable. Film samples recur like half-remembered conversations, simultaneously comic and unsettling, while Bouncyduck’s finely crafted electronic productions move between house-inflected warmth and increasingly immersive techno rhythms. The result is an album that feels deeply personal without becoming confessional, finding meaning in cultural memory rather than grand statements. Yet beneath its playful surface lie darker undercurrents. Tracks such as “Trauma” carry a palpable sense of anxiety and emotional strain, reflecting the pressures and routines that shaped the album’s creation. The closing “Homeless” is particularly affecting: inspired by the sight of a homeless man searching through rubbish during a winter rainstorm, it channels empathy rather than despair, transforming a moment of social reality into one of the record’s most powerful pieces. Its melodic, Arabic-inflected techno suggests not hopelessness but a heightened awareness of the fragility and value of ordinary life. Given the geopolitical context one might expect a ponderous album. Instead It’s Either Me or My Auntie refuses to separate humour from seriousness. For Bouncyduck, comedy is not an escape from reality but a means of navigating it. The absurdity of the film mirrors the absurdity of lived experience, while repetition becomes a mechanism for endurance rather than entrapment. Even at its most melancholic, the album remains animated by affection and gratitude. In the end, this is a record about survival through culture, memory and laughter. Beneath the loops, and dance rhythms lies an artist finding ways to remain open to the world. For all its darker shadows, It’s Either Me or My Auntie ultimately feels warm and generous. To find out more we reached out to Bouncyduck for an interview conducted over vocal messages on Instagram. But before we get to hear from him directly here’s a mix Bouncyduck has created for Svitlo Radio. Bouncyduck – The Life Of A Survivor Hi Osama, thank you for joining us. Your new album It’s Either Me or My Auntie takes a well-known Egyptian comedy and transforms it into something hypnotic, obsessive, and at times unsettling. What first attracted you to this film, and what made you feel it could serve as the foundation for a techno-oriented experimental record? It’s Either Me or My Auntie has been a part of my life since childhood. I’ve probably watched it sixty times. Every time my grandmother came to visit, I would put on the DVD and watch the film again. It became one of those things that simply stayed with me and became part of who I am. One day, while I was on a bus heading to work, I thought: why not combine techno—the genre I’ve always wanted to make—with the experimental ideas I was interested in, and blend them with my favourite movie? I used to listen to some Japanese experimental records that incorporated advertisements and fragments of found media into the music. I don’t even know what genre you’d call it, but I loved the approach. So I thought, why not do something similar with this film? As for whether I felt the film could serve as the foundation for a techno-oriented experimental record—I honestly never thought about it in those terms. I just did it because it felt right. photo by Bouncyduck Across the album, snippets of dialogue function almost like recurring thoughts rather than narrative elements. The liner notes describe them as “intrusive thoughts” embedded within repetitive structures. How did you approach sampling and manipulating the film’s audio, and at what point did humour begin to mutate into something darker or more haunting? I actually made the entire album musically first and only added the dialogue afterwards. The way I work is that I name every track very deliberately. Every title has a story behind it. The music follows the title, not the other way around. I usually start with a name and then create the music around it. Once the music was finished, I went through the film and selected lines that fit the story or feeling of each track. I chose dialogue that reinforced the intention behind the music. As for the darker humour, I think that’s just part of my personality. I’ve always had a dark sense of humour and probably always will. So if the comedy turns into something more unsettling, it wasn’t necessarily intentional. I simply chose the lines that felt right and helped tell the story I wanted each track to convey. You write that the album was made during a period when everything felt “stretched—mentally, emotionally, politically.” How do tracks such as “Trauma,” “No Means No,” and “Homeless” reflect that state of mind? Were these pieces tied to specific experiences, or are they more abstract emotional landscapes? At the time I was working in a supermarket while learning Hebrew because I wanted to improve my language skills and eventually get into university. I had a very strict routine. Every day I had a list of things I needed to accomplish: work, make music, learn how to draw, study the language, and keep improving myself. My life was extremely structured. I hardly went out at all. Ironically, my mind was actually very clear during that period. I even stopped smoking for nine months because I wanted that sense of clarity and focus while making the album. Every song on the record was intentional. Even a track like “Homeless” came from a specific experience. It was winter, and I was on a bus heading home from work while it was raining heavily. I saw a homeless man searching through a garbage bin for food. It suddenly hit me that I had a home, food, and basic security, while this man had none of those things. That moment stayed with me. So no, these tracks aren’t abstract emotional landscapes. They always come from something concrete and meaningful. photo by Bouncyduck One of the most interesting ideas in the album is that the Palestinian reality is present without being directly stated. Rather than slogans or explicit references, it emerges through repetition, tension, and a feeling of being trapped in cycles. How conscious was this approach, and do you think music can sometimes communicate political realities more effectively through atmosphere than through direct representation? You’re right, and I’m glad you noticed that. I actually dislike stating things directly. I’m also a filmmaker and animator, and one of the first things you’re taught is: don’t tell—show. I don’t want to give listeners facts or explain everything. I want to create an experience and let them arrive at their own understanding. I have the tools to make people feel something, and for me that’s much more powerful than simply telling them what to think. When someone explains a situation to you, you might understand it intellectually. But when you experience even a small fragment of that feeling yourself, it stays with you. You don’t forget it. That’s why I prefer atmosphere, emotion, and suggestion. It’s my way of communicating through music. Looking across your recent work—from Palestine Is Always War and In the Life of a Palestinian Prisoner to Blue Is the Only Color I See, Hello World Bye World, and now It’s Either Me or My Auntie—there seems to be a shift from overtly documentary and political themes toward more psychological and internal forms of expression. Do you see this latest album as a continuation of those earlier concerns, or does it represent a new chapter in your artistic practice? Actually, It’s Either Me or My Auntie was made before Blue Is the Only Color I See and Hello World Bye World, although it came after Palestine Is Always War. So I don’t really think of it as a shift. It’s more a reflection of the state of mind I was in while making the album. I never approach my work thinking, “Now I’m moving from political themes to psychological themes.” I simply make whatever feels honest at that particular moment. Every record contains a part of me that people don’t normally get to see. That’s really the only constant. I don’t think in terms of artistic chapters. I just create whatever represents me at that point in time. Humour plays a surprisingly important role on this record. The source material is comedic, yet the album often feels anxious, claustrophobic, and emotionally charged. In a context where everyday life can be marked by uncertainty and pressure, what role do absurdity, comedy, and laughter play for you personally? Can humour itself become a form of resistance or survival? Humour plays a huge role in my life. It’s how I communicate difficult truths. I’ve always used comedy as a way of talking about serious things. Life feels absurd to me. I’ve spent years reading Albert Camus and other absurdist and existentialist writers, and they’ve shaped the way I think. Questions about why we live, how we find meaning, and how we deal with suffering have always been important to me. Because of that, I often use humour as a vehicle for difficult emotions and uncomfortable realities. If you approach someone directly with heavy subjects, they might listen, but the impact is different. Humour creates another way in. It makes ideas memorable. It allows people to engage with difficult truths without immediately rejecting them. My music is very personal, and I always try to be honest. I never lie. Sometimes the truth isn’t delivered directly—it comes wrapped in jokes, laughter, or absurdity. People often think I’m just being funny, but the people who know me best understand that my jokes aren’t really jokes. They’re simply another way of telling the truth. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — The sudden and cascading beauty of this album has elevated it to the ranks of the most esteemedprogressive rock releases of the 2010s, with a lush and mournful sound that defies tradition andconjures up some of the most heartbreaking melodies to have come out of Anathema. This is, ofcourse, the album 'We're Here Because We're Here', which happens to be the Liverpudlian band's eightstudio release and first studio collection of all-original material since 2003's 'A NaturalDisaster'. This is also where female singer Lee Douglas, sister of drummer John Douglas, joined theband as a full-time member, having previously appeared as a guest on preceding releases. As for thealbum itself, written primarily by Daniel Cavanagh, 'WHBWH' is where Anathema perfected the balancebetween alternative riffs and atmospheric beauty. An album about love and death, an album with asprawling sentimental feel, and one dedicated to melodic discovery - this is precisely where it allcomes together for this band.The ten tracks appearing here vary in length, with a few reaching the seven- or eight-minute mark,adding up to some fifty-eight minutes of stunning art rock. Opener 'Thin Air' sets an intimate,melancholic tone with its sweeping guitars and pulsating percussion, while the beautiful vocalsdeliver a dose of bittersweet heartache. The song 'Summernight Horizon' then introduces a hypnotic,almost angsty riff, set against a vivid piano, while the male and female voices complement eachother gracefully on top. Third track 'Dreaming Light' reverts back to more ambient textures, while'Everything' re-ignites the album's uplifting energy with some gentle riffs. 'Angels Walk Among Us'continues the thread of elevated, quasi-spiritualistic alternative rock, with yet another stunningchorus, while the shorter piece 'Presence' seemingly concludes the first half of the record on acalmer note. 'A Simple Mistake', seventh on the tracklist, then picks up a haunting melodic build-upthat sees Anathema at their most compositionally mature. The sound of this song is exalted andmoving, and the same applies to 'Get Off, Get Out', a song that distantly echoes 'Fear of a BlankPlanet', at least in my ears. The album closes off with two intense and instrumentally peculiarsongs - 'Universal and 'Hindsight', the latter of which is a dreamy, almost symphonic-ladencomposition with ghostly vocals from Lee Douglas.I continue to be amazed by this album. Its sheer beauty is something I cannot comprehend, and eventhough it is a record I do not play so often, every new listen is simply delirious. Out ofeverything I have heard from Anathema, 'We're Here Because We're Here' is their crowningachievement.

"The Arousing" (2:50) an obvious "intro" song, it's just too Smooth and cinematic for my tastes: sounding more like soundtrack music for some American television show. (4.375/5)2. "Reviviscence" (7:00) flowing directly from the previous "introductory" song without break, I do not like the weak sound and volume coming from Gregg Lee's bass nor the weak/distant sounds coming from Alex Acuna's drums. The rest of the band is fine--up to their usual quality of performance (though they do feel a little rote/uninspired: as if they've played this song a million times and are tired of it). (13.25/15)3. "Mosaico" (7:00) here we get some Stanley Clarke feel from Gregg Lee, and some Chick Corea from Eduardo del Barrio, giving the music a bit of a RTF/Chick Corea sound and feel (which can never be a bad thing). Jorge Strunz even fills some of the song's numerous spaces with some very fine Al Di Meola-like acoustic guitar work (only with nylon stringed guitars as well as steel), which is very impressive, but where the song comes up a bit short is with any kind of cohesive themes or melody lines. Also, I just don't like the Smooth Jazz saxophone lines (and sounds) coming from Steve Tavaglione (which I know were the in-demand sounds of the era due to the popularity and success of artists like David Sanborn, Jay Beckenstein, Najee, and Kenny G). Still, I cannot find total dissatisfaction with anything this well imitative of Chick-Corea-like complexity. (13.25/15)4. "Magewind" (1:34) piano, harp, and full orchestra, sounding like some excellent soundtrack music from a 1950s film. (4.625/5)5. "Crosscountry" (5:24) this one comes across as a kind of combination of Earl Klugh, Bob James, and Spyro Gyra. It's not bad: very well performed (from some challenging charts, I have no doubt), and I don't mind the slips into orchestral Disco palettes--it's rather pretty--but something just feels a bit too pop-oriented. Still, I can't help but rate this one upward for its conglomeration of stellar individual musicianship. (9/10) 6. "Passages" (7:30) there is a problem with the levels of the individual tracks in the mix of this song that bothers me despite the fine performances from all of its musicians. Also, the composition, as admirably complex as it is, lacks enough hooks and melody for me to engage (it uses a bit too much dissonance and atonality for my tastes). In the fifth minute the high strings sustained note bridges the band's leap into a "Birdland"-inspired motif in which Gregg Lee's fretless bass and Eduardo's PolyMoog go a bit crazy (not unlike a Jaco and Jan Hammer duel). (13.25/15)7. "Dreamborne" (1:40) a nice and impressive classical guitar solo from Jorge Strunz. He is definitely a virtuoso: one of the finest players I've ever heard. (4.625/5)8. "Shanti" (4:00) with wordless female vocalese, this Disco-funk tune feels like something from one of those orchestra-enhanced artists who specialized in covering recent pop hits (this one being an Earth, Wind & Fire tune). In the end it sounds like one of the anthemic vehicles that DAVID SANBORN used to gain fame and popularity. (8.875/10) 9. "Horizon's End" (8:18) an interesting four-part tune whose themes are split pretty evenly between the eight minutes. The first is one of those Latin-infused repeating four-chord circle-dance tunes with repeating guitar riff providing the foundation for everyone else to parade over. In the third minute the motif straightens out into something more RTF-like: Power Fusion with lots of flashy soloing helping to fill the numerous pregnant spaces and pauses as well as some awesome Mahavishnu/RTF-like whole-group flurries and runs. At 4:30 there is a long pause of dead silence before Jorge enters with his classical guitar to inject a different kind of Latin flavor with a little guitar-plus-flute interlude before the band suddenly appears in toto a minute later to leap into a speedy five-chord motif over which Steve's flute and Eduardo's electric piano fly along over the racing support crew beneath. The best song on the album--the one that sounds the most like peak quality Third Wave Jazz-Rock Fusion. (18.25/20)Total Time 43:20Where I don't necessarily love the overall feel that this album's music leaves me with, I am in true awe of the amazing musicianship captured in these tracks--including George Del Barrio's amazing orchestral inputs/arrangements. Everyone of these musicians needs to be included in our lists of great musicians for their individual virtuosities. B+/4.5 stars; other than the first two songs, we have here another near-masterpiece of incredibly-well-engineered music from these amazing musicians.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Brasilian band's sophomore album release comes a year after their debut. Recording in Los Angeles with Earth, Wind & Fire's Larry Dunn in the production booth meant the guest appearances of some notable American musicians and some additional orchestration on some of the songs. The album was released by Capitol Records on April 28, 1977.1. "Sky Islands" (6:12) quite good poppy/melodic Smooth Jazz Funk that sounds as if Earth, Wind & Fire had stuck to the wordless choir vocal-instrumental format and palette of their 1975 breakout album, Gratitude. It's infectious and so enjoyable/danceable even if it is at times sounding a little dated and shlocky! Nice reckless-abondon guitar shredding from Jorge Strunze in the fifth minute. (9.75/10)2. "Ancient Source" (4:33) an awesome pop-Jazz tune with a gorgeous, melodic, and very impressive lead vocal from Diane Reeves. The easy-going orchestra-enhanced Latin foundation is sublime. (9.75/10)3. "It Used to Be" (1:14) Eduardo del Barrio's piano solo with flutey synth embedded within. (4.375/5)4. "Pegasus" (4:59) another pop-jazz tune that has a Urszula Dudziak/Michal Urbaniak feel to it as well as some amazing sound clarity due to the advanced electric engineering techniques being taken advantage of. It is definitely founded in Latin/Brasilian traditions, complete with awesome acoustic guitar solo in the second and third minute and two piano tracks in the keyboard solo in the fourth. Lite, rhythmically-engaging, and upbeat, it's a little too 1980s World Music, missing something. (8.875/10)5. "Carnavalito" (4:52) Eduardo's synth-generated pan flutes match the pan flute lines of Steve Tavaglione as the song unfolds like something from early Chick Corea/Return To Forever only more fluffed up with Smooth Jazz sounds and effects (soprano sax, rhythm guitar, occasional near-Disco riffs). Another nice exhibition of lead guitar in the fourth minute as the band stalls beneath with two chords being put on repeat. Synths and horns solo freely as vocal "hey!"s accent the final minute's music as a horn section might. Interesting but a little too schmaltzy to be included in Third Wave fare. (8.75/10)6. "Seraphim (Angel)" (4:47) now we get to something that feels like a cover of a vocal-led Soul pop songonly this one has no vocals, only flutes, synths, hand claps, acoustic guitar, orchestra strings, tenor sax, and exploding funky bass notes/riffs (piano, rhythm guitar, drums, & percussion are less forward, more background/support). Very pretty and soothing in a funky-groovin' way. (8.875/10)7. "Indigo Fire" (1:08) an impressive ANT PHILLIPS-like acoustic guitar duet from Jorge Strunz. (4.875/5)8. "Triste" (6:51) another gorgeous Smooth Jazz Funk sound palette that sounds like instrumental EW&F, only with the support of orchestra strings and more Jazzy solo options from soprano sax, electric piano, and "dirty" electric guitar. GREAT Smooth Jazz base, though. (13.333/15)9. "Pescador (Fisherman)" (1:05) the percussionists solo song (with inclusion of Eduardo's odd squeaky synth sounds). (4.375/5)Total Time 34:32B+/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of wonderfully-rich Smooth Jazz. Really enjoyable music. Highly recommended if you want to create the ambiance of a breezy Caribbean island beach cabana scene.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A debut record from a band of West Coast (California) musicians that was recorded and mixed at Hollywood Sound in Los Angeles in July of 1976 and then released by Capitol Records later in the year.A1. "Guanacaste" (6:31) a song that seems to say "Disco is here so you might as well enjoy it--in the instrumental form as well". The band produces a very nice, tight weave of the entire ensemble with catchy, if pedestrian, melodies and great engineering and production. (8.875/10)A2. "Coastin"' (4:42) bass, drums, novelty rubber duck synth notes, female vocalese, clavinet, guitars and saxophone are all added, almost one at a time, until a break at 1:40. When the band returns their fun-funky motif is used to support a searing electric guitar solo from Jorge Strunz (the same Costa Rican guitarist who would, in the 1980s, become one half of the acoustic guitar duo that would become one of the globe's most popular/famous World Music bands, Strunz & Farah). I like this unusual song. (9/10)A3. "Exaltation" (6:52) there are some really great parts to this (like the awesome bass, rhythm guitar, and percussion lines in the fourth and fifth minutes) but there area also some passages that really drag (like the third minute). I like the pairing of the synth and female vocalese in the final minute to create a kind of Michal Urbaniak-Ursula Dudziak effect. (13.125/15)B1. "Synesthesia" (7:45) the only song the album that is attributed to only one composer (Jorge Strunz), the guitarist is prominent but gives up the lead shine to his sax, electric piano player, and trombonist in lieu of himself, which is admirable, and Steve Tavaglinoe, Eduardo Del Barrio, and Raoul De Souza, respectively, do not disappoint. In the sixth minute Jorge finally takes his turn, supplying a solo that reminds me quite a bit of Cervello and Nova lead guitar phenom Corrado Rustici, which is quite impressive. It's a fine song; if only it had more hooks and earworms. (13.25/15)B2. "Out Of The Blue" (4:46) a more laid-back Smooth Jazz piece of Funk Lite that sounds as if it could have come from Bob James's production studio or the Laws family: finely crafted, extremely well performed and engineered, rolling the listener through some great hooks that have become staples for the Pop Jazz world. (9/10)B3. "El Juguete" (8:31) the album's final song has an awesome racehorse start straight out of the gate: cruising along until the band has to reign things in with a bridge to show off its whole band unity and precision, flute and guitar mirroring one another in the lightning fast melody line that ends the long bridge. At this point the band settles into a slow tempo as trombonist Raoul De Souza takes the lead but then about 15 seconds into his solo the band ramps up into fifth gear with bass, percussion, drums, and electric piano really flying along beneath Raoul's 'bone! At 3:30 there is a tag to hand off the lead to Steve Tavaglione and his flute as the rest of the band retools and gradually regains its high-speed momentum. This is awesome! So fun! So rollicking and carefree! It's almost like being on a train or rollercoaster! And Steve is an awesome flutist! In the sixth minute the band slows things down again to a trot while Jorge solos frenetically with a mean distorted guitar tone. Again the band slowly rebuilds its tempo to breakneck speed and full breadth of participation from everybody on board until they bring the party to a raucous close together at the end. My favorite song on the album--one that deserves the highest praise for its representation of top quality Third Wave Jazz-Rock Fusion. (19.125/20)Total Time: 38:40A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of mostly high quality Third Wave Jazz-Rock Fusion.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 978Gentle Giant was a British prog band that was formed in London and that was active until 1980. Gentle Giant was formed of a blues based and later psychedelic band named Simon Dupree & The Big Sound, in 1970. It featured the multi-instrumental Shulman brothers Derek, Ray and Phil. They joined with the guitarist Gary Green, the keyboardist Kerry Minnear and several drummers Martin Smith, Malcolm Mortimore and the most consistent of all John Weathers. Gentle Giant was one of the most innovative and technically complex bands of the British progressive rock movement of the 70's. Although they never achieved the commercial success of bands like Pink Floyd or Genesis and having had a short life, they are now considered a gem of the genre for their compositional rigor, a true paradigmatic prog band."Prologue" is a double live album of Gentle Giant that was released in 2003. Originally, this material circulated only as a bootleg. The recordings are from two distinct performances in the 70's: Munster, Germany on April 5, 1974. It fills the entire first disc and the first three tracks of the second. Philadelphia, USA on October 10, 1975. It occupies the final four tracks of the second disc. The repertoire is focused on the band's golden era. It has tracks from "Gentle Giant", "Acquiring The Taste", "Three Friends", "Octopus", "In A Glass House", "The Power And The Glory" and "Free Hand". "Prologue" has fourteen tracks. "The Runaway" and "Experience" were originally released on "In A Glass House". "The Runaway" has rich varieties of styles and textures, melodic, complex and creative. It's a great track, one of the best by the band. "Experience" is inventive with a complex structure. It's an example of the band's medieval complex sound. It also has other varied forms of music. It's rich with wonderful vocal harmonies. "Prologue" was originally released on "Three Friends". "Prologue", as its name indicates, gave its name to this live album. It progresses nicely with great performances especially with strong keyboard riffs and an excellent bass line. "Funny Ways" was originally released on "Gentle Giant". It's a mellow track with a nice exploration of several instruments, classic and acoustic, and electric too. It's relatively complex, a perfect example of their unique sound. "Knots" and "The Advent Of Panurge" were originally released on "Octopus". "Knots" is one of their most complex and intricate tracks. It's an avant-garde track exploring a cappella vocal style. It's a perfect example of the great vocal work of this band. "The Advent Of Panurge" is full of energy, varied melodies and different singing styles. It's apparently chaotic where all instruments seem to be played in different directions. But, it has an excellent harmony. "Nothing At All" was originally released on "Gentle Giant". It begins as a soft and nice acoustic ballad with melancholic harmonies, but that grows as a hard and heavy rock track. It's one of the most interesting tracks by the band. "Plain Truth" was originally released on "Acquiring The Taste". It's a solid rock track with the typical Gentle Giant's sound with good vocal harmonies. It's an accessible track without great complexity and more traditional. It's less typical than usual. "In A Glass House" was originally released on "In A Glass House". It's excellent with great harmony. The chorus is of superior quality. It has a hard rock section with a memorable guitar riff. This is also an amazing track. "School Days" was originally released on "Three Friends". It's nice with experimental vocals and musical passages. It has the use of several instruments at the same time. It also has beautiful piano work, one of the best performances by Kerry Minnear. Phil Shulman sings wonderfully. It's also one of his best vocal moments. "Intro/Cogs In Cogs" was originally released on "The Power And The Glory". It's another excellent track with complex multi-part vocal harmonies. It has an intricate orchestral arrangement. "Excerpts From Octopus", as its name indicates, has excerpts that were originally released on "Octopus". It includes significant parts and solos based on five songs from the original album: "The Boys In The Band", "Raconteur Troubadour", "Dog's Life", "Knots" and "The Advent Of Panurge". The medley is amazing, one of the greatest testaments to Gentle Giant's musical genius and technical virtuosity on stage. "So Sincere" was originally released on "The Power And The Glory". It's a complex and dissonant track. It's experimental and avant-garde with jazz influences. It has certain nonsense, a rather exquisite song. "Free Hand" was originally released on "Free Hand". It's an elaborate and complex track. It's a traditional Gentle Giant's track with some dissonant parts and with constant changes of rhythm and tempo, in the Gentle Giant's style.Conclusion: As I mentioned above, "Prologue" is an "official bootleg" live album from Gentle Giant, as happened with some other live albums released by the band. At this moment it comes to my mind two: "Interview In Concert" and "King Alfred's College Winchester". From what I remember, I own these two live albums too, "Prologue" is probably the one that has a better sound. I agree with Badabec. There is just one track that has a really bad sound quality: "School Days". Of the others, the sound is acceptable or even good. And the sound quality is the only reason I don't give it 4 stars. The track list is excellent and is well representative of the band, and the performance is amazing too. So, 3 stars.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by Matti — This is the debut album of the Swiss harp-playing artist often categorized as New Age. Seemingly it has been released internationally only in the 2-CD set The Trilogy, which I purchased in 1992 soon after discovering Vollenweider's charming music from library. The album info here misses the track titles, but perhaps they weren't in the original LP then. The Trilogy in turn misses several parts of the suite.The main difference to his later works is the greater amount of guitars, both electric and acoustic. Also I feel, despite the "suite" form, that these highly melodic pieces are more solidly standing as individual compositions whereas many albums usually proceed in a conceptual, voyage-like continuity, where picking up single tracks is quite irrelevant. This is definitely not to say that this suite would miss continuity. On the opening piece 'The Shepherd' (I) Andreas plays harp, ocarina, guitar and soprano sax, creating a piece full of atmosphere, colour and progressivity. 'The Gate Within the Gate' (II) builds from it with a bigger combo of musicians. Max L�sser's electric guitar and the strong rhythm section guarantee the emotional increase.'Her Cat Dance' (IV) features the light, jazzy groove typical for the later output. 'The Letter' (V) is a brief and classically oriented solo piano piece, followed seamlessly by 'Little Boy and the Mirror' (VI) where soprano sax and synths carry the lighthearted melody. There's a hint of Pekka Pohjola or Bj�rn J:son Lindh. 'A Walk With My Father' (VII) is starring Andreas' father on church organ, joined later by Andreas' ocarina. Such a profound depth in this piece. 'Summer Rain' (VIII) is a tiny, light jazz piece highlighting piano and electric guitar. A bit like Pat Metheny. 'Desert in the Horglass' (no numbering, possibly not on the original LP) is a serene, 51-second track for harp, soprano sax, alto flute - and cello which makes me think of the New Agey music of David Darling. This piece ends the version of "The Art Suite" heard on The Trilogy. My apologies for reviewing an album on basis of an incomplete listening experience, but it deserves being revisited nevertheless. Any friend of Vollenweider's personal music would be fortunate if coming across this apparently rare album.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Though Caldera recorded most of their albums in LA, they were a NYC band, filled with members fromall over Latin America and the US. Developing a torrid fusion between Jazz-rock, jazz-funk, Latinjazz , Caldera was a typical product of its era, somewhere between Return To Forever and (to alesser extent) Weather Report, but with added horns. However, the album's sleeve might be a tadmisleading, as you won't find much African in the music. The Latin side doesn't translate much in aSantana world, though. Their music is almost all instrumental,; though there are some appearance ofa female singerThe musical excellence of every band member at their respective instruments was even more impressiveand enhanced by clever songwriting that sometimes approached climates close to progressive rock.Caldera's compositions sometimes reached breakneck speeds, much like RTF, not only by the guitaristStrunz, but also by Del Barrio's choice of the then-modern synths that were more Zawinul's type thanCorea's. Odd thing is that the wind instruments of Tavaglione and De Souza softened the tone andgave it a "soul-ier" feel.With a track like Coastin', one can think of HH's HH (Head Hunters) aswell.Complex, while somewhat relaxing, it's a bit of a headscratcher as to why Caldera"s album flew underthe radar of most aficionados, while the inferior Spiro Gyra attracted much more attention.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — After a promising start with their serf-titled debut, Caldera brought high expectations, sporting an erupting volcano, that wouldn't be met, since the album is drenched under syrupy string arrangements, coupled with ill-advised female vocals (Diane Reeves) in the album's introduction, though it works fine in the excellent Ancient Source.Triste is more straight-forward almost smooth-jazz (this didn't exist back then), while Indigo Fire is a short Flamenco guitar interlude. Seraphim is probably the album's weaker moment, though, again drowned in string arrangements.Nevertheless, if you manage to ignore those "flaws" (orchestrations and vocals), the band is back with its original brilliance and flawless tightness and progressive climates.

items.body: Review by SilverLight59 — Returned to the Earth's fifth studio release, Stalagmite Steeple is a heavy, dark, yet gorgeous concept album. Rising up from the lingering shadows of the Covid-19 pandemic, the story traces an elderly couple separated during lockdown; the wife passes away alone in a care facility, while corporate billing predictably continues uninterrupted. Rather than exploding in aggressive rage, Returned to the Earth channels this injustice into a quiet but intense, tragic beautiful piece of art rock.Looking at the album cover, we see that the tone of the album is aptly captured in its foreboding atmosphere and presentation. Emphasizing the album title's imagery, the artwork mirrors the bleak, slow-evolving nature of a stalagmite, a structure built drop by drop over vast stretches of time, isolated in the dark. This serving as a perfect parallel companion piece to the lyrical concepts inside. It's a warning to the listener that what lies within is an exploration of the abyss, lacking bright colors but rich in deep, shadowed contrast, if we dare explore there.My first introduction to Returned to the Earth was their preceding album Fall of the Watcher. This came across as melodic and polished neo-prog, but it still maintained an adjacency to mainstream art pop structures making it quite accessible. Stalagmite Steeple on the other hand, shifts the paradigm entirely. It is noticeably more low-key, heavily melancholic, and unhurried than its predecessor. The album abandons any residual desire to please radio formulas, steering entirely into a unified, esoterically somber atmosphere. Where the previous record felt like a collection of beautifully produced, individual statements, this new one winds out as a single, unified journey that takes considerable effort to fully absorb. In short, if you are hoping for Fall of the Watcher part two, you may be disappointed.That being said, Returned to the Earth is quietly building a body of work that is weaving atmospheric musical landscapes and lyrical tapestries that reach the listeners emotions and psyche. Led by singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist Robin Peachey, alongside Paul Johnston and Steve Peachey, the band is creating its own unique space in the prog universe. Notably, with each release, they have been moving more and more to reject hyper-technical, "mile a minute" instrumental showmanship in favor of spacious, slow-burning compositions allowed to breathe and unfold at an organic pace. With Stalagmite Steeple, this is truer than ever. If this is your cup of tea, this will satisfy your expectations in a big way. So let's take a brief look at the tracks.1. Dark Morality (7:19)The album opens with probably its most accessible track, its flagship single, perfectly setting the slow, plodding thematic tone that will largely be a precursor for much of the album and the songs within. Driven by a deliberate, descending chord progression and a heavy, chugging bass line, the song allows Peachey's warm, clean vocals to come to the fore and really shine. The guitar work for the final couple minutes slowly grows in intensity with a bit of a Porcupine Tree groove to it. There is an expectation for it to totally break loose, but instead it fades out which is a bit of disappointment, but a fine track nonetheless. One other minor complaint, the first thirty to forty seconds of this track is entirely inaudible, which I find to be very annoying. (8.5/10)2. The Final Time (5:00)A profoundly mournful ballad addressing the literal moment the album's subject passes away, isolated from her family. Sorrowful orchestration underpins the track, again with gradual build up, then a full drop off in pace, and finally a soaring, crying guitar solo cuts underneath the mix to articulate the grief being painted. (8/10)3. Stalagmite Steeple (9:58)The title cut and the near-ten-minute centerpiece. This opens with an unhurried, hypnotic, cyclical piano line and low key lyrics. At the 2:30 mark, big guitar line changes the mood. While overall the track builds with restraint, the layering expressive guitars and a floating melody instrumental section elevates the emotion. About midway the music strips back down to the opening piano and lyric motif. As has been mentioned by others, there is similarity with the style of Tim Bowness lyrically, and indirectly, Steven Wilson musically here. The final two minutes begin once again to escalate the intensity. The structure is nice, but once again there is the thought that it may break open, but restraint is the coda here, as this one also fades out to finish it off. (8.25/10)4. Meaningless to Worth (6:09)Acting as the thematic pivot, this track transitions from the couple's personal perspective to the broader social failures of the pandemic era. It is incredibly subdued and reserved for the first two minutes, then drums and synth wash enters raising the tone, at three minute guitars enter. At four minutes the full rhythm section finally lands, and builds up a nice intensity which plays out to the end. (8.5/10)5. Die for Me (9:09)The second longest track. Starts with a wobbling synth wash. Yet another slow build, but the vocal quickly lifts this track up. Guitars come in underneath and this starts to become the most dynamic and structurally propelled track on the record. There is a calming pause midway which rebuilds the track and introduces an even busier, electronic rhythm track that breaks up the album's prevailing understated essence, culminating in a powerful, shuddering guitar solo that vents genuine anger at the institutional systems that failed society. This one actually opens up at the end and builds to a big finale we have been waiting for. (9.75/10)6. The Raging Sea (5:36)The album closes not with a continuation of the dramatic storm, an intense final statement, but rather with a velvety, calming melody meant to offer a sense of resolution. The ebb and flow of the music featuring a lovely guitar lead and warm bass lines mimicking the tides, pointing toward an ideal of natural peace where humanity must eventually return after trauma. The emotional floating vocal melodies over the atmospheric soundscape closes out the album with an overarching sense of resolution and hope. A very nice and accessible track for the finish. (9.5/10)So, what is the final takeaway at the end of the day? While Stalagmite Steeple is a triumph of tasteful atmosphere, pristine production, and emotional resonance, a realistic critique must note what some may see as its limitations. Because the band is so wholly committed to a deeply meditative low-key mood, the album can occasionally feel restrictive in its expression . Listeners who crave shifting time signatures, aggressive rock bombast, or instant melodic payoffs may find themselves waiting for a musical explosion that never arrives. The songs intentionally build beautiful foundations but sometimes refuse to "dress" them with standard rock climaxes. It requires a measure of patience and the right, introspective headspace to fully appreciate the soundscapes being developed. Ultimately, I really like what is going on herein, and I am of the opinion that Stalagmite Steeple is a bold progression for the band as it doesn't rest on being an extension of their last album, but will stand alone as a unique and singular milestone. It is totally different, and as such, a brave, carefully constructed, and elegant exploration of human grief. Perhaps not the happiest of subjects, but a worthy one given the times that we live in. For those willing to slow down and unplug from the fast-paced and largely insensitive world we are all part of, and submerge themselves in its reflective lyrical depths and methodical musical expressions, it functions not as a depressive wallowing in grief, but in the end, a nurturing, healing, uplifting message of reconciliation. You may need to be in the right mind set to take this one in, but it is well worth the effort. 4 deeply reflective stars.

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — Spinetta...the thousand sounds man, he is distinctive for his long standing tradition of startingbands, releasing some masterpieces then ditching them and starting a new one, this was the case forInvisible, chronologically, Invisible is his fourth band after the collapse of Pescado rabioso(which had practically, by the release of Artaud, become his solo project). Therefore, this, asInvisible's debut album, will have a somewhat transitional and tense sound, almost as if the new andold band identities were playing tug of war, this, which in theory, should harm the record, actuallystrengthens it's quality, since it creates an organic, vivid mix of Pescado rabioso's folk,acoustic, surreal and sensitive textures with the symphonic, grandiose, experimental and jazzy soundof Invisible...this is a recipe for a listen that is engaging in every possible way, filled withlittle details that require time to fully digest and understand fully, therefore, this is alsoincredibly relistenable.(It's absolutely worth noting that, Invisible is a supergroup just as ELP was, this will influencetheir releases significantly as they're much more intricate and technical than other Spinettarecords)One of the things that separates this record from other Spinetta releases, is it's accessibility,not much of his music is quite accesible and easy for the casual listener (even as he had hits andfame, most of his music remained too Avant Garde for the general public), this would be inherited byInvisible's final record "El jardín de los presentes" 2 years later. Some of the compositions arequite art pop just like Alan Parsons! The opening track "Jugo de lúcuma" comes to mind regardingthis, the clean guitar tones, sensible playing style, and the balance and dynamics betweeninstruments create textures that can be felt like landscapes that shift each second, just like aplacid, deep sleep that induces you in a beautiful, whimsical dream.The strongest feat of the record is the musicianship, as mentioned above, this is a supergroup, eachmember knows when to attack, paint and when to step back, therefore the compositions are not bloatedand each note can be heard crystal clear, it's a ship that's democratically run and sails through aglowing ocean, you can feel the angle the pick plays the strings and the flick of the wrist thedrummer makes each bea..their chemistry is quite organic and flows naturally, you can tell theywere all quite disciplined on their playing but also.paid attention to delivering emotion, each onesynchronized perfectly with the other.I can't say much about the compositions that hasn't already been said, after all it's Spinetta whowe're talking about. But I will say some things regardless of that, since I do have quite some stuffto tell you, about the way this music feels.The compositions are creative and sensitive! You can feel as if you were there, sitting on a field,during a starry evening in the argentinian Pampa. The music is sensitive, chill and playful, almostlike a beloved childhood memory, Spinetta was a poet before he was a musician, so the music alsotells a story even if the lyrics are absent, what better example than "Azafata del tren fantasma"?It really captures the essence of the poem! It has influences of jazz fusion but they're not overlyon your face, the influences are pretty balanced which highlights the creativity of the compositionsand the uniqueness of it's sound, and since it's a transitional record, it also has that cutesurreal Artaud vibe to it! Can't say much more, Spinetta is just a genius composing.The lyrics are narrative, surreal and personal, contrasting Artaud's dark, gritty and angst filledlyrics, these are rather playful and even optimistic, a complete shift in attitude, nonetheless,they're just as poetic and introspective as Artaud's. The thing that is most enjoyable about theselyrics are the way they tell stories, in a Realismo mágico (Magical realism) Cortázar way, quiteLatin American! Lovers of that literature style will love these!Amazing production, balanced, crystal clear...Overall, it's a record that's worth every single second and dollar if you get to buy it! A uniqueexperience that everyone should feel at least once in their lives.

items.body: The opening of “You Only Live Twice” is one of the most famous John Barry ever wrote: violins dropping two octaves in a run that sounds Japanese but is pure Western scale. He wrote it for the fifth Bond film in 1967, Leslie Bricusse wrote the words, and Nancy Sinatra sang it at CTS Studios in London over a 60-piece orchestra. The melancholy French horn line underneath it was Barry’s too, though he borrowed that from a Tcherepnin piano concerto. London-based The Lo-Tones turn that theme into dub reggae, shrinking the 60-piece score to a small session on brass and keys with the bass sitting heavy underneath. Behind it are Felix Howard, one of British pop’s most established songwriters, who co-wrote the Sugababes’ breakthrough “Overload” and has written for Amy Winehouse, Sia and Kylie Minogue before moving into A&R, now heading it up at Kassner Music, and Tim Hutton, a multi-instrumentalist who has played with the Prodigy, Groove Armada and Above & Beyond since he came up through the anarcho-punk bands The Mob and Zounds on Crass Records. Nick Manasseh mixes it, pulling instruments out until the sub-bass does most of the work: he built his first sound system in 1985 and cut “Seventh Seal”, widely called the first UK Steppers record, three years later. Lovelle, a south-east London singer trained at the Mick Jagger Centre and Sylvia Young, sings Sinatra’s old part low and close to the groove. Manasseh also runs off a full dub version, dropping the vocal and letting the bass and echo carry the track on their own. Stream and listen to “You Only Live Twice” HERE The post Daily Discovery: The Lo-Tones – You Only Live Twice (feat. Lovelle) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Stiff as a board, light as a feather You held me up forever I should really let go A chunk of my heart and soul Portland post-punk band Darkswoon return with a high octane remix of “Thread,” the lead single from their fourth LP Antivenom. The remix hails from renowned New York City DJ, producer, musician, and engineer Hi-Fi Hillary, aka Hillary Johnson, head of Kale Shelter Studios. While the original version of “Thread” is a powerful, yet melancholic guitar-driven anthem on love and loss, the remix kicks the song into overdrive, replacing Darkswoon’s shoegaze-inspired guitars with bubbling synth pads and injecting the song’s steady beat with electronic sound and fury. Despite this, vocalist Jana Cushman’s deeply warm and honest vocals add intimacy and vulnerability to the track. As such, the remix is perfect for both the dance floor as well as a long, meditate sunset drive. Darkswoon and Johnson first met during the pandemic as guests on Johnson’s Kale Shelter Twitch streaming series, spotlighting veganism the underground music scene. Johnson’s many credits over the years include recording/engineering work for bands such as Bootblacks, Liste Noire, Second Still, Angels of Light, Autodrone, My Favorite, and Bell Hollow, the latter which she also played live keyboards with. She has also recently remixed tracks by Astari Nite, Black Rose Burning, Frenchy and the Punk, IKON, and The Long Losts and has upcoming remixes scheduled with Negative Agent, and The Harrow. She will also be appearing as part of 2026’s Murder of Crows DJ Lineup. Proceeds for this remix will be donated to Animal Aid PDX, a no-kill animal shelter where Cushman has been volunteering at for thirteen years. Be sure to check them out if you live in the area. Otherwise, listen to the track below and stay tuned for a new split 7” release from Darkswoon and Altar Girl to come later in 2026. items.body: I’ve been a ball of fire in your arms desireAnd I’ve been wondering, where it is you’re hiding Gene Loves Jezebel will celebrate the 40th anniversary of their breakthrough third studio album, Discover, with a newly remastered and expanded double-LP reissue arriving July 24 through Beggars Banquet. The collection pairs the original 10-song album with Glad To Be Alive, a concert recording captured in Nottingham in 1986, included as a bonus LP with initial copies of Discover. The live set returns to vinyl here for the first time since that original pressing, while an expanded digital edition will present the complete 17-song performance. The label has offered an early preview with “Desire — Live in Nottingham,” a particularly charged performance of the single that became Gene Loves Jezebel’s calling card. James Stevenson’s familiar guitar introduction quickly gives way to a faster, rougher reading, with Jay and Michael Aston trading and tangling their voices over the band’s relentless momentum. Listen to “Desire — Live in Nottingham” here. And watch the official music video for Desire below: Originally released in 1986, Discover found the Welsh band Gene Loves Jezebel widening their reach of the gothic rock and post-punk heard across Promise and Immigrant. Chiming guitars, forceful rhythms and the Aston twins’ competing voices gave the record a sharper melodic profile, carrying the band from the independent underground toward an international audience. “Desire (Come and Get It)” stood at the center of that advance, joined by “Heartache,” “Sweetest Thing,” “Over the Rooftops” and “Beyond Doubt.” The record retained the tension and theatricality of the band’s earlier work while opening the songs into larger, increasingly direct forms. “This is the album where it all came together for me as a singer & a songwriter,” Jay Aston says. “I discovered myself.” Michael Aston adds: “Feelings with no ceilings, and the thinnest things are a joy forever.” The Aston twins began making music together in 1980, initially working as Slav Arian with guitarist Ian Hudson and a drum machine. Raised in Porthcawl, South Wales, they relocated to London the following year, where the project developed into Gene Loves Jezebel and signed with Beggars Banquet imprint Situation Two. The anniversary edition has been remastered by Henry Rudkins and will be issued on double black vinyl with updated artwork. The first 200 orders placed through the Beggars Banquet store and Bandcamp will include two postcards signed by Jay and Michael Aston, while supplies last. Discover/Glad To Be Alive: 40th Anniversary Expanded Edition arrives July 24 through Beggars Banquet. Pre-order the release here. items.body: Rare DM Attention self-released New York’s Rare DM, nee Erin Hoagg, has been a going concern in the broader world of synth music for some years now, plying a tasteful take on modern electro, with some darker overtones. 2026’s Attention feels like something of a departure for the performer and producer in that it sets aside much of the project’s urbane sensibilities for more direct and naked emotion, and more forceful and stripped down songcraft. Importantly, the musical side of the record feels consistent with Rare DM’s catalogue to this point, just more insistent, and frequently more nervy and even anxious. That manifests via the fast moving bass and tumbling drums of “LA Traffic”, its synths detuning and jumping around between its percussive change ups, and the cod-acid techno of “Significant Other”, a song whose grinding rhythm and machinegunned bass seems more likely to inspire panic attacks than dancing. That said, there are plenty of more subtle indicators of where the project is at these days to be found as well; on the simple synth ballad “Lil DM”, much of the project’s busy production and layers of electronics are stripped back, replaced by one of the best vocals they’ve recorded, swimming through big atmospheric reverbs in ways that feel vulnerable and dreamy in equal measure. It’s those moments where we finally get a slightly clearer picture of who Hoagg is, beyond the bounds of their stylized persona. There’s always been a certain coy detachment apparent in previous recordings, and despite her obvious vocal charisma, we were never able to get much of clear read on who Rare DM is. Songs like “Mean Girled” and “Feel Nothing” simply sound more candid then we’ve come to expect from her; the former right from its confessional opening couplet (“We’re not even fucking/Why am I worried about you?”), the latter for its obsessive repetition, that gets more manic until the whole song goes into a shaky meltdown. It’s still obviously the same artist, and the production is still the same mix of darkwave, minimal synth and general art pop, just amplified, and, well, more blunt. Attention is well-named, especially in how it feels like the most magnetic that Rare DM has sounded. There’s a few drop dead gorgeous cuts (twinkling closer “Landed” is absolutely tremendous for one), and a few club bids (the archly delivered “325”), but they all serve to paint a broader and more detailed portrait of Rare DM, compellingly so. Buy it. Attention by Rare DM The post Rare DM, “Attention” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: (Image via Pexels) We announced it a while back, but we are finally ready with the results from our survey on the use of AI in the dark music scene. In this article we will present you the results of that survey we did in March 2026 involving 821 respondents from the darkwave, EBM and industrial music scene. The survey was done after Bandcamp banned AI music from its platform. The group of 821 people were those who answered our request for completing a survey that was initially sent to 1641 people randomly selected from our database of 4217 musicians, journalists, visual artists, photographers and other creative professionals from the dark music scene. All answers were treated anonymously, which was an important condition to get as many results returned as possible since the AI stigma is all around as this Facebook post shows. Important, our editorial team did not participate in this survey in order not to distort the results as several are AI specialists and / or consultants in their daytime jobs where they build AI flows and AI agents. However, the results from the scene professionals indicate clearly that the use of AI is very present in all layers of the scene. Below are the results of this survey in detail, and we also explain how the survey was executed, plus we checked it with other studies to have a clear benchmark. PS: We did use AI in order to visualize the results below, so there isn’t any misunderstanding :). The survey itself Background Artificial intelligence has entered most parts of music production and promotion. Musicians use it for audio restoration, stem separation, administration and idea development. Journalists use it for transcription, translation and editing. Photographers automate selection and image correction, while artwork designers face growing competition from generative image systems. This study shows how a survey of 821 darkwave, EBM and industrial professionals turned out taking in account the distinctive values of these scenes: independence, human authorship, recognisable visual identities and resistance to standardised commercial production. The survey applied two scene-specific assumptions. First, dark-scene professionals would use AI heavily for self-managed tasks such as translation, social media, artwork preparation, editing and administration. Second, they would show lower acceptance of complete generative replacement because authorship, imperfection, subcultural identity and recognisable personal style carry substantial value within these genres. These assumptions have now been verified for the first time through a dedicated darkwave, EBM and industrial survey. Methods A sample of 821 professionals was divided across six occupational groups. Adoption probabilities and attitudes were crosschecked against independent surveys of music creators, journalists, visual artists and photographers. The results eflected the self-managed and visually driven nature of the dark alternative music sector, but they do also correspond with wider music scene changes and adoption. The questionnaire covered professional background, AI usage frequency, applications, perceived benefits, economic consequences, copyright, transparency and attitudes towards AI-generated work. Results An estimated 63.7% of respondents had used an AI-assisted tool during the previous 12 months, while 47.3% had used generative AI. Weekly use reached 31.8%. Adoption varied sharply by profession. It was highest among photographers and video creators at 84.4%, followed by producers and engineers at 82.0% and journalists at 78.8%. Artwork artists and graphic designers recorded the lowest adoption rate at 43.6%. Despite broad practical use, 88.8% wanted human authorship to remain central. More than 90% supported consent, compensation and labelling requirements. Only 5.9% of current AI users had generated a complete musical track with AI. Conclusion of the survey The model predicts neither wholesale rejection nor unconditional acceptance. AI will probably emerge as an established backstage tool within the dark music sector, particularly for repetitive and administrative work. Resistance will remain strong wherever AI replaces authorship, imitates a recognisable style or uses protected work without permission. 1. Background research behind the AI in dark music survey The music sector has moved beyond the question of whether professionals use artificial intelligence. The more relevant questions now concern which tools they use, which tasks they delegate and where they draw ethical boundaries. A study commissioned by GEMA and Sacem, based on a survey of more than 15,000 music creators and publishers and published in January 2024, found that 35% of music creators had already used AI in their work. Adoption reached 51% among creators under 35. At the same time, 64% believed the risks outweighed the opportunities, and 71% feared that AI could threaten their ability to earn a living. Concerns have continued to rise. A PRS for Music survey published in February 2026, based on responses from more than 2,630 members, found that 79% of creators worried about AI-generated music competing with human work. Another 76% expected AI to affect their livelihoods negatively, and 92% demanded greater transparency from AI services. AI adoption also differs widely between creative occupations. Research from the Reuters Institute involving 1,004 UK journalists, surveyed between August and November 2024, found that 56% used AI professionally at least once a week. Transcription and captioning were the most common tasks, used at least monthly by 49% of respondents, well ahead of AI use for drafting article text. Visual artists show greater resistance. A Society of Authors survey of its members, conducted in January 2024, found that 12% of illustrators had used generative AI. A quarter of illustrators, 26%, reported losing work because of AI, and 37% said the income from their work had decreased in value because of it. A separate DACS study involving 1,000 artists found that 74% were alarmed at the prospect of their work being used to train AI models without consent or compensation. Ninety-five percent wanted to be consulted before their work was used for training, and 94% wanted financial compensation for that use. Photography presents a different pattern. A VSCO survey of 401 photographers, fielded in December 2025 and published in April 2026, found that 83% used some form of AI in their workflow. Among working professionals, 68% used it weekly or daily, roughly double the 34% rate among enthusiasts. Much of this use involved culling, editing, administration and workflow management rather than replacing the photographer’s creative decisions. These differences are important in the darkwave, EBM and industrial culture. Music, photography, graphic design, journalism, performance and personal identity frequently overlap. A musician may also run a label, design merchandise, edit videos and write promotional material. The scene therefore offers a useful case study of how AI enters small, interconnected creative economies. 2. Research questions The survey addressed six questions: How many dark-scene professionals would report using AI? Which professional groups would have the highest adoption rates? Which tasks would professionals delegate to AI? Would AI use correspond with more favourable attitudes towards it? How strongly would respondents support consent, compensation and disclosure? Which professions would report the greatest economic pressure? 3. Methods of the Side-Line survey Study design A 39-item questionnaire was specified, covering professional role and experience, age group, frequency of AI use, generative and non-generative AI use, task-specific applications, time savings, quality and reliability, economic effects, copyright and training data, voice, image and style imitation, disclosure and labelling, and future adoption intentions. Attitude statements used a five-point Likert scale ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree.” For the principal analysis, “agree” and “strongly agree” were combined. Definition of AI The questionnaire distinguished between two categories. AI-assisted tools included automated mastering, noise reduction, stem separation, transcription, image culling, object removal, translation and language correction. Generative AI referred to systems that produced new text, images, voices, video or music in response to instructions or uploaded material. This distinction prevents routine tools such as intelligent noise reduction from being treated as equivalent to generating an entire song or cover image. The sample of the survey Each respondent received one primary professional category, even when multiple roles would normally apply. Primary professional roleRespondentsShareMusicians, composers and performers33240.4%Journalists, editors and broadcasters13216.1%Artwork artists and graphic designers11714.3%Photographers and video creators9611.7%Label, PR, promotion and booking professionals9411.4%Producers, sound engineers and mastering professionals506.1%Total821100% The age distribution reflected the audience and professional history of darkwave, industrial and EBM which corresponds largely with the audience of our Facebook page. Age groupRespondentsShare18-3416920.6%35-4424129.4%45-5424730.1%55 and older16420.0% 4. Results of the survey Overall AI adoption Of the 821 synthetic respondents, 96 used AI daily (11.7%), 165 used it weekly but not daily (20.1%), 262 used it occasionally or monthly (31.9%), 95 had tried AI but stopped using it (11.6%), and 203 had never used it professionally (24.7%). Current AI adoption therefore reached 63.7%, or 523 respondents. The modelled 95% interval was 60.4% to 66.9%. Generative AI use was lower at 47.3%, or 388 respondents. The interval was 43.9% to 50.7%. Weekly or daily use reached 31.8%. These results suggest that AI would already be common in the scene, but not necessarily central to the creative process. How often dark-scene professionals use AI (n=821)Weekly/daily use 31.8%Occasional/monthly 31.9%Tried, stopped 11.6%Never used 24.7%Breakdown of AI usage frequency among 821 darkwave, EBM and industrial professionals. Adoption by professional role Professional role had a clear relationship with general AI use while the role also affected generative AI use. AI adoption by professional roleAny AI useGenerative AI usePhotographers and video creators84.4% · Any AI use55.2% · Generative AI useProducers and engineers82.0% · Any AI use56.0% · Generative AI useJournalists and editors78.8% · Any AI use59.8% · Generative AI useLabel, PR and promotion professionals70.2% · Any AI use55.3% · Generative AI useMusicians, composers and performers54.2% · Any AI use41.9% · Generative AI useArtwork artists and graphic designers43.6% · Any AI use31.6% · Generative AI useAI adoption by professional role, comparing any AI use against generative AI use. Photographers and producers recorded high adoption because AI functions have become embedded in editing and production software. Artwork artists showed the lowest adoption and the strongest resistance to image-generation systems. Journalists occupied a middle position. They used AI frequently, but mainly for processing existing material rather than replacing reporting or criticism. Age differences Generative AI adoption declined with age. That relationship was statistically clear within the matrix. Generative AI use by age group18-3460.9%35-4451.5%45-5442.5%55 and older34.1%Generative AI use by age group, declining from 60.9% among 18-34s to 34.1% among respondents 55 and older. The youngest respondents were about three times as likely to use generative AI as respondents aged 55 or older when comparing their unadjusted odds. Age did not eliminate ethical concerns though. Younger users remained strongly supportive of consent and labelling, even while reporting higher adoption. What professionals used AI for Respondents could select multiple applications. Percentages in this section use the 523 current AI users as the denominator. The pattern supports a clear distinction between assistance and replacement. What dark-scene AI users do with it (n=523 current AI users)Proofreading, rewriting or translation61.0%Image correction, culling, masking or upscaling47.0%Brainstorming and concept development45.7%Transcription, captioning or subtitles41.1%Social posts, SEO, press copy or administration39.6%Audio cleanup, mastering assistance or stem separation36.7%Audience analysis or release planning22.8%Generating complete artwork16.4%Generating musical elements, voices or stems15.7%Generating a complete musical track5.9%What AI users in the dark music scene report using it for, ranked by share of current users. AI was used most often to process, organise or improve material created by a person. Complete generation remained uncommon among professionals. Differences between occupations Musicians most often used AI for promotional copy, translation, troubleshooting, demo preparation and audio restoration. Producers from their side concentrated on noise removal, stem isolation, restoration, audio-to-MIDI conversion and mastering assistance. Journalists used AI for transcription, translation, headline development and grammar correction. The us of AI for complete review or interview generation remained low. Especially in this section we wonder if the lack of the most basic flow creations is due to a lack of programing knowledge or something else. This was however not asked in the survey, but it is clearly food for another survey. Photographers reported extensive use of automated selection, denoising, sharpening, masking and object removal. Fully synthetic concert or artist photography remained rare. Artwork artists used AI for references, layout tests and concept exploration more often than for final covers. Many avoided image generators because of copyright concerns or fears that their visual style could be replicated. Label and PR professionals used AI primarily for translation, metadata preparation, scheduling, campaign variations and administrative work. Perceived benefits The strongest positive finding concerned routine work. 71.9% agreed that AI was useful for administrative or repetitive tasks. Among weekly users, 62.5% estimated that AI saved at least two working hours per week, with a median estimated saving of 3.1 hours per week. Of AI users, 45.7% used it during brainstorming, and 38.9% said AI helped them complete work they would otherwise have postponed. Only 9.4% believed AI-generated creative material consistently reached professional quality without substantial human editing. Among respondents who generated text, images or audio, 56.2% said correction, selection and fact-checking sometimes consumed as much time as the initial generation. The productivity advantage therefore depended on the task. AI performed best where the desired outcome could be checked quickly. It performed less reliably when the work required factual precision, scene knowledge or a recognisable artistic identity. Human authorship Support for practical AI did not translate into support for autonomous creation. Overall, 88.8% wanted human authorship to remain central. 78.6% worried that AI would make music and artwork more homogeneous, and 74.2% believed excessive AI use would weaken the relationship between an artist and the audience. 64.6% would be less interested in a release marketed as fully AI-generated, while 57.9% accepted AI-assisted work when a human remained responsible for the concept and final result. This distinction represents the central outcome of the survey. Respondents did not judge every AI application in the same way. Correcting noise in a live recording received far more acceptance than generating a singer’s voice. Translating an interview received more acceptance than producing an interview that never took place (yes, this is something that happens in the music business, more than you think). Copyright, consent and transparency The strongest agreement occurred around creators’ rights. Support for consent, compensation and transparency (n=821)Voice, image and identity rights require protection94.0%Consent required before training use93.4%AI companies must disclose training sources92.7%Fully AI-generated work must carry a label92.2%Creators must receive compensation91.1%AI-assisted editorial content needs a clear policy82.5%Agreement with statements on consent, compensation, labelling and transparency for AI use. These estimates align with broader creator research. A UK Music report on AI found that over 90% of surveyed creators supported consent, payment, labelling and protection of an artist’s voice and image, while two-thirds said AI poses a threat to their careers. The survey also found that 67.7% would consider using an AI service built entirely on licensed material. This result challenges the idea that creative resistance stems from a rejection of technology. Much of the resistance concerns how existing systems obtain material and distribute economic value. Economic pressure Overall, 27.4% reported an experience of lost assignments, lower rates or increased client pressure attributed to AI. The relationship between occupation and economic pressure was clear. Economic pressure attributed to AI, by role (n=821)Artwork artists and graphic designers43.6%Photographers and video creators37.5%Journalists and editors26.5%Labels, PR and promotion25.5%Musicians and composers20.8%Producers and engineers20.0%Share of respondents reporting lost work or rate pressure attributed to AI, by professional role. Visual professionals faced the greatest modelled pressure because posters, social graphics, promotional portraits and low-budget cover assignments can be replaced more easily than performances or complex music production. Respondents were more concerned about the erosion of smaller commissions than the immediate disappearance of established professional roles. This reflects a broader economic warning. A study by CISAC and PMP Strategy, published in December 2024, estimated that generative AI could place 24% of music creators’ revenues at risk by 2028, a cumulative loss of around 10 billion euros between 2023 and 2028. This is an economic forecast and it illustrates the scale of the possible substitution effect. Training and organisational policies Only 13.5% of respondents had received structured AI training. Just 18.6% worked with an organisation, publication, label or band that had a written AI policy. Among respondents using AI for editorial or promotional work, 58.3% always checked factual claims, 26.7% checked them only when the subject appeared unfamiliar, and 15.0% (!) had no consistent verification process. The gap between adoption and governance represents one of the clearest practical risks. Professionals have started using tools faster than organisations have developed rules for accuracy, disclosure, confidential information and copyright. 5. Discussions that will follow after this survey gets out AI is normal backstage but disputed onstage The survey shows that AI use is already normal within the dark music sector. However, most use remains invisible to the audience. We also assume that not all respondents did really show the back of their tongue as far as AI adoption goes. Professionals use it to remove background noise, separate stems, transcribe interviews, correct text, translate announcements, organise photographs and prepare campaign variations. Far fewer allow AI to become the named composer, artist, photographer or journalist. This creates a practical boundary: AI receives acceptance as infrastructure but gets a clear resistance as authorship. The underground scene has strong reasons to automate Darkwave, EBM and industrial projects often operate with small teams. One person may handle recording, mastering coordination, artwork, social media, merchandise, advertising and distribution. AI can reduce the burden created by this do-it-yourself structure. Its value becomes clearest in work that consumes time without defining the artist’s identity. For an independent band, translating a press release into four languages can make a measurable difference. Generating the band’s music, photographs and visual identity raises an entirely different question. Visual professionals face the earliest commercial pressure The results place artwork artists and photographers at the centre of economic disruption. Their resistance should not be interpreted as a lack of technical knowledge. These professionals often understand image-generation systems precisely because they see how quickly clients can replace smaller commissions. The same professional may use AI denoising or automated masking while rejecting a model trained on unlicensed artwork. Tool adoption and opposition to current commercial practices can exist at the same time. Full AI music remains separate from professional adoption The number of fully generated tracks entering streaming platforms has increased rapidly. Deezer reported that fully AI-generated tracks exceeded 50% of its daily uploads at peak level in June 2026, reaching approximately 90,000 tracks per day. That supply however does not prove widespread professional acceptance. In this survey, only 31 of 523 current AI users had generated a complete track. Most musicians preferred tools that modified or supported their work rather than replacing composition and performance. The difference between platform volume and professional practice is important. Automated upload systems can produce large catalogues without representing the working habits of established artists. Ethical licensing could change adoption More than two-thirds of the respondents would consider licensed AI tools. That creates a possible route for the industry: publish training-source information, obtain permission from rightsholders, compensate creators whose work supplies the models, protect voices, faces and artist identities, mark fully generated material clearly, and preserve human responsibility for professional output. These measures would not end every objection. But, they would address the concerns that currently block adoption for many professionals. A reality check for the broader audience who is opposed to the use of AI This survey of 821 darkwave, EBM and industrial professionals revealed a sector already using AI extensively but selectively. Professionals embrace AI where it removes repetitive work, improves damaged material or helps small teams manage large workloads. They resist it where it replaces human authorship, imitates an artist’s identity or depends on copyrighted work collected without consent. The expected dividing line runs between AI as a controlled professional tool and AI as an unaccountable substitute for creative labour. Within the dark music underground, the technology’s future therefore depends less on its ability to generate more content and more on whether it can operate without erasing the people, rights and identities that gave the scene its value. Note that this survey did not assess which roles face the greatest risk from AI. Broader studies indicate that many jobs are already under serious AI threat.
