items.body: Label: Self released, 2026 Personnel - Jay Matharu: guitar, keys; Erik Brandell: tenor saxophone; Christine Lanusse: bass guitar; Jacob Johnson: drums. Jay Matharu is an eclectic British-born guitarist and composer living in Uppsala, Sweden. His bold sound reflects a strong connection to metal—he’s a member of the band Liv Sin—but Disillusion marks a turning point in his solo career, weaving prog-rock, fusion, jazz-funk, and R&B into a patchwork of influences shaped through carefully crafted arrangements. Each member of his quartet—tenor saxophonist Erik Brandell, bassist Christine Lanusse, and drummer Jacob Johnson—recorded the album’s eight original compositions remotely. The music emerged from Matharu’s Master’s research in Music Performance. “ Atrophy ” is introduced in waltz time by Matharu, who is soon joined by Brandell as the music pivots into a 4/4 funk excursion. Both musicians splash a multitude of colors across the fluid rhythmic tapestry before returning to the opening 3/4 meter. “ Bare ” keeps the ternary feel alive, aligning saxophone and guitar in stimulating parallel lines. Brandell’s solo, imbued with adventurous melody, eloquence, and energy, invites us into compelling jazz fusion territory. “ Cog ” reveals classical influences within a theme receptive to subtle tempo shifts. Johnson’s snappy drum fills carry a prog-rock attitude, pairing naturally with Lanusse’s popping bass grooves. The piece is fueled by Matharu’s chromatic runs in a thought-provoking meeting point between Joe Satriani and Rez Abbasi. The Indo-jazz-rock thread runs even deeper in “ Chalo ”, a kaleidoscopic mosaic unfolding through ten-beat cycles and paying tribute to Matharu’s late mentor, sitar player Pandit Sanjay Guha. While “ Deluge ” features a memorable theme, a touch of Latin elation, and the bandleader’s metal-inflected soloing, “ Butterflies ” is a rewarding odd-metered exercise driven by throbbing bass lines and strong melodic development. The blazing guitar solo unfolds over a septuple-meter backdrop before launching into a metal-jazz romp fueled with high-octane energy. Throughout the album, Matharu and his band periodically reinvigorate the proceedings, with the closing “ Bittersweet ” standing as another fine example of dramatic shifts in rhythm and mood, moving from R&B soulfulness to jazz-funk audacity while leaving ample room for the drummer to stretch out. Although the ideas on Disillusion emerged from improvisational exploration, the whole outshines the parts. Matharu is following a promising path. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Atrophy ► 02 - Bare ► 07 - Butterflies

items.body:
A decade into his career, TEN celebrated the milestone the best way he knows how — on stage. Across TEN:CORE0110, the Thai superstar's sold-out three-night residency transformed Thailand into the centre of his ever-growing universe, bringing together fans for a career-spanning spectacle that looked back on his journey while hinting at what comes next.

Opening with 'Nightwalker' — the track that signalled the beginning of his solo era — TEN wasted no time setting the tone. The performance flowed seamlessly into fan favourites including 'ON TEN', 'Birthday', and 'Shadow', each elevated by intricate choreography, cinematic visuals, and polished production that highlighted his reputation as one of pop's most dynamic performers.

The energy only climbed higher as grooves from 'Dangerous', 'Enough For Me', and 'Water' had the audience on their feet, before shifting into more emotional territory with 'New Heroes', 'Butterfly', and 'Lie With You'. By the time 'Bambola', 'Sweet As Sin', and 'STUNNER' arrived, TEN had delivered a set that showcased not only his versatility but also the artistic evolution that has defined his past ten years.

The residency became even more memorable thanks to surprise appearances from NuNew, PiXXiE, NONT TANONT, Jeff Satur, and PP Krit, each joining TEN on stage to celebrate the landmark occasion and turning the anniversary into a celebration shared with friends and collaborators.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by PiXXiE (@pixxie_official)

The biggest surprise, however, came on the final night. TEN unveiled 'If You Don't Mean It' live for the very first time, giving fans an exclusive preview ahead of its official global release on 27 July. As the concert reached its finale, one final reveal awaited the crowd: a cinematic teaser announcing 'OUTWEST', his upcoming English-language single slated for release in September.

More than a retrospective, TEN:CORE0110 felt like a statement of intent. While the residency celebrated the achievements that have established TEN as a global performer, it also made one thing clear — the next chapter is already underway, and he's stepping into it with the same ambition and artistry that have defined his first decade.

items.body: In November 2023, tellKujira found themselves in Paris during a residency at IRCAM while workers at the Centre Georges Pompidou were protesting outside, demanding the protection of their rights. Entering a space dedicated to artistic and technological innovation while hundreds of people faced the prospect of losing their jobs proved a disorienting experience, and La lucha è un poema collettivo is framed by that encounter. Although rooted in this particular episode, the record continually opens onto broader questions surrounding solidarity, collective action, and the ways music can respond to political experience. The opening En grève begins in what feels like experimental improvisation, integrating field recordings and a cut-up, looped speech in Castilian about solidarity before veering in unexpected directions. Layers of strings accumulate with intensity, building toward a rapturous and abrupt collapse that gives way to the viola slipping into an enveloping mood of softness, something that feels almost like reconciliation after confrontation. The piece embodies the group’s interest in shifting perspectives: samples, instruments, and textures interact revealing contradictions and tensions. Mexican field recordings return in ¡Que viva México!, a brief but evocative interlude. Rather than attempting to represent Mexico, the piece captures something of its overwhelming sonic density, where human presence itself becomes a form of resistance. Guitars and strings then move to the foreground in the counterintuitively titled Tarantella, which avoids any easy recourse to Southern Italian folk quotation. Instead, cyclical arpeggios introduce a hypnotic and incantatory mood. By the time we reach the closing Walking on the Beach / What to Love and Fight For, the album has already guided the listener into a contemplative state. Plucked strings, a giggling child, gentle guitar lines, and field recordings create a richly textured sonic field in which different acoustic suggestions pull the ear in multiple directions at once. Fragments of poetry surface and dissolve without ever coalescing into a stable narrative: “I like walking on the beach / we cannot stop / with closed eyes / unrevealed secrets / to be 16, 14, 15, 40, 100…” Memories, desires, and possibilities drift in and out of focus. The listener is left to assemble their own meanings from these scattered traces, until the album suddenly comes to a close on a single breath taken. This is a beautifully produced album, rich in texture and detail. Without romanticising struggle or reducing politics to slogans, La lucha es un poema colectivo acknowledges that there is no truly non-ideological listening position. Instead, it frames activism, solidarity, and collective experience in ways that invite reflection rather than prescribe conclusions. Through its intricate layering of field recordings, instrumental interplay, and fragmented texts, the album asks listeners to actively participate in the album and assemble their own connections between sounds and ideas. In doing so, it transforms listening from a passive act into a form of engagement, rendering La lucha es un poema colectivo not simply a record about collective action, but a genuinely participatory experience. To tell us more about the production process, tellKujira (Ambra Chiara Michelangeli – Viola, Francesco Diodati – Guitar, Francesco Guerri – Cello and Stefano Calderano – Guitar) have kindly answered a few questions via email. The title La lucha es un poema colectivo (“The Struggle Is a Collective Poem”) emerged from your experience at IRCAM while workers at the Centre Pompidou were protesting outside. How did that encounter shape the album? Did it change the way you thought about the relationship between artistic creation and collective action? The album title does not refer exclusively to the Centre Pompidou protesters. Rather, those words are part of an artistic path that has always led us toward a vision of music as a tool for sharing and transformation. You will not find, in our music, solipsistic moments aimed at showcasing individual virtuosity; instead, there is an attempt to actively guide the listener into that process of secondary creation that emerges through immersive listening. One example can be found in the central section of “En grève”, a very long passage built around layers that gradually accumulate in intensity, where this invitation becomes almost explicit. The same process, the same attention, can be found throughout the entire album. The opening piece, “En grève” (“On Strike”), unfolds over more than sixteen minutes and seems to inhabit a space between tension, endurance, and solidarity. How did you approach translating the atmosphere of a strike into sound, and what role did improvisation play in shaping the piece? “En grève” emerged from a plurality of materials. Some of them—particularly the instrumental ones—had been developed over the years preceding the recording of the album, during rehearsals and concerts, while others were created during our residency at IRCAM. This extended period of experimentation and creation in Paris, far from our usual habits, made it clear that there was an urgent need to adopt a new creative process, one in which the surrounding context could enter forcefully into the work. It was an exhausting compositional effort, one in which it was very easy to fall into clichés or predictable solutions. What you describe as the “atmosphere of a strike” was created by making instrumental ensembles, samples, tapes, timbral textures, and harmonic structures interact as though they were figures in a Cubist painting. The point of view is constantly shifting; contradictions and opposites emerge; samples are brutally cut and edited; there is no veneer intended to make things sound pleasant. Then, at the peak of this process, the perspective turns inward and opens onto the viola’s final song. It is a heartbreaking, minimal melody that arrives like a punch to the stomach after nearly ten minutes of gradual approach, bearing witness to one of the most intriguing aspects of human nature: passion, love, and tenderness persist within us; they may hide, but they do not disappear beneath the sound of shouting voices and drums. As for improvisation, although this ensemble is very familiar with improvisational language, I do not think that “improvisation” is the right term in this specific case. The pieces are highly structured, and every element—even the smallest nuance—carries a carefully calculated weight. It is important to stress that, from the outset, we decided that this would not be, unlike our first album, a record based solely on performance. We were interested in creating a work that was heavily shaped through post-production. We liked the idea of extending our interplay through all the possibilities offered by studio work. In live performances, we strive to recreate this balance with great precision, and to achieve that our setup has expanded considerably, incorporating samplers and synthesizers. “¡Que viva México!” references Sergei Eisenstein’s unfinished 1930–32 film project, a work that has been described as both his greatest artistic ambition and his greatest personal tragedy. What drew you to Eisenstein’s abandoned vision of Mexico, and do you see any parallels between the film’s unfinished nature and contemporary political or artistic struggles? The unfinished can be beautiful when it leaves room for imagination and becomes fertile ground for both our own fantasies and those of the listener. We began from a purely musical process, creating a symmetrical counterpart to “Tarantella,” and later worked with additional arpeggios and field recordings collected in Mexico to express our own perspective. The perception of a place can be highly subjective—like the game of partially covering your ears in order to focus on certain sounds rather than others. Quite naturally, we were drawn to the kaleidoscopic humanity reflected so intensely in the sounds that literally overwhelm anyone visiting those places. It becomes a form of human resistance to the political forces that continue to devastate Latin America and the societies that compose it. “Tarantella” is an intriguing title because listeners might expect a direct engagement with Southern Italian folk traditions, yet the piece seems to avoid any obvious folkloric quotation. What interested you about the idea of the tarantella, and how did you reinterpret its cultural and symbolic associations without relying on folk material itself? The title emerged during the composition of the piece and refers in particular to the cyclical movement of the arpeggio and to a certain hypnotic repetition that is never exactly the same twice. This becomes the red thread of a journey through moments of disorientation and lyrical passages that contrast with the central riff. As with the other pieces, we were not pursuing a specific aesthetic goal, but rather an inner meaning that could be reflected in music as directly as possible. To achieve this, we worked extensively on details, stripping sounds bare. What initially appears to be a simple arpeggio gradually reveals a sense of estrangement and, at the same time, physical resistance—a struggle with the instrument itself. In this sense it recalls the endless tarantellas described in the writings of Ernesto De Martino, which captured the attention of the tarantolato and induced a trance-like state intended to expel the spider’s venom. The relationship between the individual—particularly women, in the case of the tarantolate—and the community becomes a struggle for life itself. A similar process can also be found in “Walking on the Beach – What to Love and Fight For,” where elements drawn from African and African-American traditions are isolated and used individually within a completely different context. The album was conceived during a residency at IRCAM, a place strongly associated with technological research and experimental composition. How did that environment influence the music? Did the contrast between the institution’s highly specialised artistic context and the social realities unfolding outside its walls become part of the record’s conceptual framework? Our residency at IRCAM and our work with Somax2—a software environment for musical improvisation and composition using AI, machine listening, cognitive memory activation models, and multi-agent architectures—were decisive. They facilitated and accelerated a process that was already underway in our artistic practice. The most interesting aspect of that period of research was precisely the effort not to lose ourselves chasing the easy illusions and mirages that often accompany new technologies. It was important to spend enough time with these tools to gain the necessary distance from them and to develop the critical awareness needed to avoid self-referential or purely aestheticizing dynamics. Allowing the real world, with all its political and social implications, to enter the work was also a way of making the best possible use of technology by placing it entirely in the service of meaning. The closing track, “Walking on the Beach / What to Love and Fight For,” ends the album with what feels like an open question and with a text/poem which seems like a dialogue between different generations or the final message of a dying person. In a time marked by political uncertainty, social fragmentation, and ongoing conflicts, what are the things that you personally believe are still worth loving and fighting for? And how does music help articulate those values? And what can you tell us about the use of field recordings and found sounds within this particular track but also, more in general, in your work? The final text is the result of merging two poems by Alice Keller and Elena Chiattelli, read by Chiara Guidi. There are many, many things worth fighting for, and just as many that deserve to be loved. Everyone has their own causes and their own struggles, but perhaps what we all increasingly feel is the need to become a community—to rediscover the signs that unite us and weave them together into a single fabric. All of the field recordings move in that direction. They emerge like icebergs from our memory and define both the space and the boundaries of the world inhabited by this album. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Photo by Gabe Palacio.   Les Arts Florissants at Caramoor July 17, 2026 Published in Sequenza 21 By Christian Carey KATONAH, NEW YORK – Les Arts Florissants are the premiere ensemble devoted to French music of the baroque era. Though they have branched out from this remit in recent years – their most recent recording is of Haydn masses – the group remains devoted to performing French opera. On Saturday, they presented two one acts by Marc-Antoine Charpentier (1633-1704), their namesake piece, Les Arts Florissants, and La Descente d’Orpheé aux Enfers. The ensemble’s dozen musicians were directed by its founder William Christie, who also played harpsichord and organ. They were joined by singers from Le Jardin des Voix, a training program directed by the tenor/conductor Paul Agnew. These may be emerging artists, but they all acquitted themselves admirably. Photo by Gabe Palacio. Les Arts Florissants was written in homage to King Louis XIV, in whose court it would have been performed. There are several references to him in the libretto, always as a proponent of the arts and bringer of peace. The Arts are represented by characters playing Music, Poetry, Painting, and Architecture, with each getting a chance to extol the virtues of their respective arts. A standout was soprano Camille Chopin, who sang La Musique with considerable grace and beauty. Soprano Sarah Fleiss as La Poésie was playful, this demeanor and her quicksilver high soprano complementing the other soloists well. Haute-contre (high tenor) Bastien Rimondi as La Peinture and contralto Sydney Frodsham as L’Architecture provided a light-hearted duet, linking their respective arts into a dynamic duo. The Arts are beset by La Discorde, played with wily verve by bass-baritone Olivier Bergeron, and Un Guerrier (War), performed by bass Kevin Arboleda-Oquendo. After their efforts plunge France into conflagration, La Paix (Peace) arrives to help restore order, extolling Louis’s protection of the Arts and his people. Josipa Bilić sang the role with affecting poise and a warm tone. Ultimately, La Paix is victorious and the Arts are restored to their rightful place at court and, by extension, throughout France. Photo by Gabe Palacio. La Descente d’Orpheé aux Enfers is one of a number of operatic adaptations of the Orpheus myth. Unlike others, it doesn’t allow for Orpheus’s backward glance at Eurydice sending her back to Hades, instead ending with them beginning their ascent from the underworld. Apparently Louis didn’t like tragedy. That caveat aside, it is an attractive work, filled with affecting music. Much of it goes to the title character, played here by Richard Pittsinger, whose haute-contre voice was both supple and substantial. He met the considerable demands of a high-lying and dramatically intense role well. Arboleda-Oquendo sang Hades with ominous gravity. Fleiss played his wife, Proserpine, a character far removed from the lightness of La Poésie. Here she performed with affecting dignity. One wished that Euridice was given more to do in the opera, as Chopin lent it considerable poignancy. Rimondi and Bergeron were joined by tenor Attila Varga-Tóth in a trio of tormented souls in the Underworld, their voices blending well in plangent harmonies. Tanaquil Ollivier as the nymph Oenone displayed an attractive lyric soprano voice. Bilić as Daphné again impressed with a captivating presence. The instrumentalists have inhabited this repertoire for a long time, and their experience and abundant talents were evident. Christie, leading from the harpsichord, elicited nimble tempos and impressive coordination from the ensemble, with considerable dynamic nuance. Although they are a chamber orchestra, Les Arts Florissants demonstrated an impressive blend of colorful timbres. The continuo group included the aforementioned keyboards, as well as archilute, violone, and bass violin, which afforded a number of different ways for the harmony to be realized. The rest of the ensemble consisted of a pair each of flutes, violins and viola da gamba players, as well as a percussionist. A particularly affecting choice made by Charpentier was to silence the violins and feature the viola da gamba players when Orpheus is in Hades. The semi-staging focused on movement, which was abetted by four graceful dancers. The singers moved quite well too. In Les Arts Florissants, the Arts were besieged by the entropy wrought by Discord and War, and even seemed to slip towards the dark side before Peace helped to reel them back in. La Descente d’Orpheé aux Enfers began with a pastoral scene, in which confetti burst aloft from white sheets and parlor games were acted out in ebullient fashion. The story turns dark, of course, and this was illustrated by the use of red cords throughout, as the snake that bites Euridice, as barriers to Orpheus’s trip to the underworld, and to bind those suffering in Hell. One question lingered; if Orpheus wasn’t supposed to look back at Euridice, why did the blocking make that all but impossible? Photo by Gabe Palacio. In his program note, Christie noted that the advocacy of Les Arts Florissants for French baroque music had yielded gains for the repertoire with other ensembles and in opera houses throughout the world. This shift is a welcome one, but Les Arts Florissants are still the best group on the planet doing Charpentier’s operas. -Christian Carey   The post Les Arts Florissants at Caramoor appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Sole (unfortunately) album from this double KB and double wind instrumental septet ogling towardsKent music, and we're not in the mode of their countrymen of De Loreans , but more in the KimioMizutani sonic realm (his sole album from the early 70's). Because, yes, we're definitely in the70's soundframe, and calling this album "retro" is irrefutable, but don't expect anything likeHatfied Health or North National. What is really clear is that, while Moleslope having their own sound, is their inspiration from SoftMachine, but around the 7/Bundles/Softs era, when Jenkins and Ratledge were both on keys, but with ahorn section to boot. And is it ever a success, because their music is irresistible. Of their seventracks of the album, six are relatively short (under 5 minutes), but inspired and jumpy, filled withenthusiasm and happiness. Of course, between the organ (my guess is a Hammond) and the electricpiano (no doubt a Rhodes), the Soft signature is evident, but both the trumpet and the sax had evenmore flavors, not even mentioning the odd flute bits (or so it sounds like it). The closing 7-mins+Little Night Trip Released in late December 2019, I had to fit this album at the very laqst minute of my top 10 albumof the year, and TBH, I cheated a bit and also selected for the next year's top 10, because it isthat good. Though the album might sound a bit samey throughout its course, it doesn't overstay itswelcome, since it last barely over 32 minutes, but exhilarating ones.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The Norwegian quartet Red Kite arrived with a prior history, yet under this name, they are forging a new sound. There is a powerful intensity right from the start of "Ptah, The El Daoud", an industrial, mechanical sound that nonetheless evokes the raw ferocity of the early Mahavishnu Orchestra. Even Helte Hermansen dives into intricate solos imbued with the spirit of McLaughlin; driven forward by bandmates Trond Fr�nes (bass) and Torstein Lofthus (drums), the music surges as if bringing down stars, until a restorative rain of keyboard work from Bernt Andr� Moen sets in, though it brings no light, as the surrounding atmosphere remains deeply dark and suffocating. It is progressive jazz."13 Enemas For Good Luck" borders on stoner rock, featuring a guttural scream that emerges from that very darkness. Nothing here is left to chance; the sounds of the four instruments are meticulously arranged to synchronize and create the specific atmosphere, the mood, in which the composition truly shines. Then comes the psychedelia, but always a musical idea that stretches, turns inside out, and changes, one part remains the same while the other constantly mutates.A touch of the chaos from Miles Davis's Bitches Brew cosmic era drifts through "Flew A Little Bullfinch Through The Window." "Focus On Insanity" opens with a drum solo that reminded me of Tony Williams Lifetime's "Red Alert," followed by a flamenco-style guitar solo accompanied by the Rhodes. The keyboard then takes over, shifting into a truly spacey sound; what I love is how they keep playing right past the point of losing the key, completely unconcerned, perhaps aware that another key lies waiting there.Torstein Lofthus might be known for Elephant9, but guitarist Even Helte Hermansen truly breaks the mold. "You Don't Know, You Don't Know" drifts away in a spiraling fade-out, suspended between heavy bass and drums and the floating textures of the keyboards and guitar. It is a debut that promises delightful surprises and sparks curiosity about the direction they will take next; without a doubt, Red Kite is a distinctive quartet with a unique path of its own.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It is good to hear something classic, something that sounds familiar yet new at the same time.That is the case with Agropelter, the Norwegian band that, with The Book of Hours, has opted for an instrumental work.There are echoes of Genesis and Steve Hackett's sound, but also new elements, such as an organ layered over a synthesizer, as heard on "Levitator.""Burial Mound" features a distinctly fusion-style fretless bass that is highly expressive; it almost takes on a solo role against the keyboard backing, yet remains supportive of the track.Finally, "The Book of Hours" is a four-part suite featuring piano work that reminded me of instrumental sections by Focus, very much in the style of Continental Europe. A highly expressive piano solo begins with Tony Banks and culminates with Rick Wakeman, before the keyboards kick the band into a symphonic improvisation.As the suite progresses, the piano, and its interplay with the Mellotron, takes on increasing importance. It is distinctly classical in nature because it employs the technique of adapting works by classical composers, much like bands from the 70s did, drawing here on Beethoven and Rachmaninoff.In the fourth section, a harpsichord appears as if fallen from the heavens, with Bach also making his presence felt, capturing the sense of space, silence, grandeur, and pathos.There is a climax created when the entire band plays together, with the keyboard soaring above them, weaving in and out of their parts; it is fascinating to hear how it draws from both classic Genesis and Steve Hackett's solo work, yet the final result is a self-sustaining piece that takes the listener on a journey, complete with introduction, development, and resolution.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — In A Fever Dream by Haken is a surprisingly great short EP from the English prog metal legends, showcasing a moodier darker sound than their previous albums. Having lost 2 members recently, the band have scaled back in their technical side to showcase more heaviness and groove, with their melodic side still intact. It's also nice to see Ross Jennings showcasing some post hardcore like shouts to accompany his screams. While I would have loved a full length from them, this presentation of a newer sound is a great palatable short affair. I'd give this a low to mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Lotus.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Distant Satellites' is the tenth studio album from Anathema - an ethereal art rock odyssey thatsees the band repeating themselves a little after finding a successful and effective formula onpreceding albums. The music on this release is atmospheric, mellow, and sentimental, and as a bandknown for masterfully merging lush and epic soundscapes, Anathema delivered one of their mostresonant studio albums ever here. However, at the same time, 'Distant Satellites' relies too much onthe heartfelt and melodramatic style that had been explored on 'Weather Systems', for example, andgenerally feels somewhat monochromatic. I can't help but think of Sigur R�s' post-rock-meets-ambientaesthetic while listening to this album, which also features an abundance of electronic sounds andprogrammed keyboards. A quality release, nonetheless, 'Distant Satellites' features strong trackslike 'The Lost Song' (of the three parts, 1 and 3 are perhaps the more intriguing ones), the gloomy'Dusk [Dark Is Descending]', then 'You're Not Alone', which is a more experimental entry that wasalso mixed by Steven Wilson, and the 8-minute-long title track, which for me perfectly captures theessence of this album. If you are into heavily atmospheric alternative rock, Anathema's 'DistantSatellites' will be a fine treat, but if you're looking for something more novel, you better listento their previous albums.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Anathema released their 'Weather Systems' in 2012, and this album has since become one of theEnglish band's most well-received and admired works. However, this is a particular album that is notan easy one to love - while it is incredibly solid production-wise, 'Weather Systems' is supposed tobe lived through and experienced emotionally, as it is also one of the most evocative progressiverock albums of the 2010s. Now, speaking of progressive rock, I've always felt like this is not thecategory that this record belongs to, as it exhibits a much stronger post-rock influence. 'WeatherSystems' also features some gorgeous string arrangements and an overall moody, atmospheric soundthat relies on slow-built instrumental build-ups and powerful vocal performances, making it more ofa post-progressive effort. One could speak of progressive arrangements perhaps, or sophisticatedinstrumentals, but this is an album that is nowhere near the traditional notion of progressive rock.Now, the bulk of the material on 'Weather Systems' was written by the band's primary songwriterDaniel Cavanagh, while his brother Vincent handled the electric guitars as well as the majority ofthe vocal duties. Interestingly enough, Jakko M Jakszyk appeared as a mixing engineer on this album,while frequent collaborator Christer Andr� Cederberg was once again hired as a recording engineer.Considering the songs on this record, there are some tracks that are truly exceptional, and others Icould barely care about, which does not diminish the fact that 'Weather Systems' is a beautifully-sounding and immersive album. Opening track 'Untouchable, Part 1' is a moving art-rocker that startsoff with some gentle acoustic guitars and then gradually climaxes into an instrumental masterclass.The epic sound of this song is finished off on 'Part 2', which has a laid-back chamber pop aestheticthat moves into a nicely orchestrated guitar-laden soundscape. 'Lightning Song' then sees a finevocal performance from Lee Douglas, as this is definitely one of the slow-burners of the album,while 'Sunlight' is where the otherwise-excellent sequence loses some steam. The gracefully flowingatmospheric soundscapes begin to drag a bit at this point.Thankfully, the second half of the album introduces some new sounds through the darker, and almostindustrial-informed 9-minute composition 'The Storm Before the Calm'. This kind of experimentalplaying mixed up with the haunting moodiness was definitely missing in the first half. 'TheBeginning and the End' then captures your attention with a warm studio sound elevated by a smoothproduction, while 'Lost Child' introduces a pervading and affecting mood that is set against acathartic ending and some cinematic soundscapes. All in all, 'Weather Systems' is a solid albumreplete with beautiful sounds and powerful arrangements, and while not every single minute of it isbreathtaking, the quality of this album is definitely immaculate.

items.body: Review by alainPP — A Liquid Landscape?opening for Anathema and Riverside?delivers a blend of neo-prog metal and post-alternative rock. It is atmospheric art rock infused with 90s energy; while Alice In Chains and Nirvana form a backdrop, the band bears a closer resemblance to Tool or even Karnivool."A Few and Far Between Part 1" features a radiant sound and alternative distortion?a fusion of Porcupine Tree and XTC set against an oppressive atmosphere. It unfolds with a progressive, latent quality reminiscent of Anekdoten, its dark side weaving through hypnotic, winding paths. The track concludes in a post-rock style that drifts away from their original sound, with a tense outro leading into the slow, Floyd-esque "A Few and Far Between Part 2." A brooding atmosphere lulls the listener, yet brilliant notes keep the senses engaged. The guitar sparkles with a hushed, psychedelic tone?perfect for contemplation?while a vocoder melts into the mix on "The Sky Moves," evoking Alan Parsons. A crescendo builds upon a swell of backing vocals, achieving a state of sublime elevation?this is what prog is all about. "Intention" follows, featuring a voice-over set against radiant, cinematic notes that straddle the line between alternative and modern prog. The melody is hypnotic, minimalist, and pastoral, building to a crescendo worthy of Anathema, before resolving into an acoustic finale of breathtaking beauty."Consequence" drives forward with a more aggressive tempo, anchored by Robert's rhythmic bassline; the feel is choppy and kinetic?a classic binary musical groove. Niels launches into a "grungy" solo?part hard rock, part hauntingly melodic?balancing sonic power with softness in an oxymoronic blend. A sharp cut leads to a cinematic outro filled with distant, enigmatic sounds. "Raven Song Part 1" begins with a dark, liturgical feel, featuring a bright, archaic guitar note. An airy, space-like interlude invites reflection amidst mysterious vocal layers. "Raven Song Part 2" enters with a high-pitched melody, echoing the style of The Edge. A pronounced, mantra-like, repetitive rhythm section; impassive vocals conveying melancholy. The sound is exploratory and progressive, captivating the listener; the track exudes a grunge vibe?thanks to the screaming vocals and heavy guitar?bordering on alternative metal, reminiscent of giants like Tool or Karnivool. "Virgo Calling" begins gently, with raw acoustic guitar accompanying a gritty vocal. A simple build-up takes a progressive-alternative turn?akin to the young French band Moonshine Blast?leading to a controlled explosion of smoldering post-rock where the riff turns metallic.A Liquid Landscape has reinvented itself with the release of this powerful progressive alternative post-rock album.

items.body: There is a historic town in southern Estonia, population 17000, that every July transforms into a global cultural hub. For four days, the ruins of its 13th-century Livonian Order Castle fill with tens of thousands of people who have come, some of them from the other side of the world, to listen to music that in some cases nearly ceased to exist. The Viljandi Folk Music Festival has become one of the largest events of its kind in the Baltic and Nordic countries, and the 33rd edition, running 23 to 26 July, may be the most internationally ambitious yet. The festival did not end up there by accident. Viljandi is where the Viljandi Culture Academy is based, the only institution in Estonia that trains folk musicians at degree level, and where the Estonian Traditional Music Centre operates year-round. The festival was founded in 1993 by the generation that had lived through Soviet occupation and understood, from experience, what song had meant in that period: it was music that carried the language and identity through fifty years of occupation, and it was mass singing that fuelled the restoration of independence in 1991. Thirty-three editions later, festival director Ando Kiviberg has said that the popularity of traditional music among Estonian youth is remarkable even by international standards, and the 2025 edition, which drew 38000 visits across four days, bore that out. Ask anyone who has been and they talk about the crowd before they talk about the line-up. A stranger gets pulled into a chain dance within minutes of arriving. Someone who has never held a kannel or a set of bagpipes can be playing one by lunchtime. A child plays violin on a street corner while the crowd moves around them. Every Estonian president since independence has attended every edition. The setting does the rest. The main stage occupies the shell of the Livonian Order fortress begun in 1224, the open-air auditorium sitting where the inner courtyard once was, with Lake Viljandi visible through gaps in the medieval masonry and a rope bridge from 1931 swaying above the 13-metre defensive trench at the hill’s edge. Nine stages across nine hectares: some outdoors on the hills, some in indoor venues through the town. The procession from the town centre to the castle on Thursday afternoon has opened every edition since the beginning. The 2026 theme, “To Each Their Own Instrument” (Igaühel oma pill), has shaped a programme of 60 artists, 65 ticketed concerts and 85 free shows across two open-access stages, plus more than 30 workshops. Festival director Kiviberg and programme director Tarmo Noormaa have pulled in artists whose work is built around a specific traditional instrument or regional playing tradition, and this year’s international reach is wider than usual. The 2026 programme reaches further than any previous edition, and some of the instruments it carries with it are ones rarely heard in the Baltics. Starting with The Zawose Queens from Tanzania. The duo, composed of Pendo Zawose and her niece Leah, performs wagogo music with the chizeze, a one-stringed fiddle, the ilimba, a wooden-board lamellophone, and ngoma drums, instruments carried through the tradition of Hukwe Zawose. Manhu, from the Stone Forest region of Yunnan in southwest China, bring a related depth of inheritance: the lusheng gourd pipes, the adiza three-string lute, the moon lute and the sanhu, a bowed instrument traditionally played to accompany storytelling, sit alongside electric bass and drums, carrying the traditions of the Sani people, a community geographically isolated from other Yi populations for long enough to develop its own distinct musical identity. Orkesta Mendoza from Tucson, Arizona, fold brass, accordion and marimba into a sound built from the border cultures of the US Southwest and northern Mexico, and Nancy Vieira introduces morna to the festival for the first time, the slow song style of Cape Verde inscribed on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list, built around guitar, cavaquinho and violin and most associated internationally with the late Cesária Évora. Vieira, born in Guinea-Bissau and raised in Lisbon, has spent two decades keeping the music close to its roots in the port towns of São Vicente That attachment to a community’s specific instruments runs through the European contingent too. Karolina Cicha from Poland performs the music of the country’s minority cultures, Tatar, Karaim and Lemko, on accordion and Polish dudy bagpipes. The Polish-Ukrainian ensemble HrayBery draw on fiddle, hammered dulcimer and frame drum to play cossacks, kolomyikas, mazurkas and polkas recovered from nearly forgotten archival scores of the Galician border region where Poles, Ukrainians, Jews and Roma have lived alongside each other for centuries; their set at Tallinn Music Week 2025 convinced Noormaa to book them immediately. They were not the only act from recent Tallinn bills to make the journey to Viljandi. Hungarian family band Amaro Duho closed the Fenno-Ugria Night at Tallinn Music Week 2026 with traditional Hungarian Oláh Roma music; the band was founded in 2021 by Matild Dobi, a co-founder of Ando Drom, when she decided the time had come to pass four decades of Roma musical experience to her children, threading their own melodies through the inherited material on guitar, tambura and accordion. From eastern Europe, the programme reaches into Scandinavia and the North Sea, where the same archival instinct takes a different form. Groupa, the Swedish-Norwegian trio active since 1981, play old Nordic melodies tuned outside equal temperament, with improvised passages and percussion cut from stone and wood. Gangar push that archival instinct harder: the Oslo five-piece dig rare tunes out of Norwegian folk archives and drive them through rock, metal and jazz, a combination their second album, released in April, extends further still. Shetland pianist Amy Laurenson, BBC Radio Scotland Young Traditional Musician of the Year 2023, whose debut album Strands was longlisted for the Scottish Album of the Year Award in 2024, brings a playing style built on an island where the piano became central to folk playing in a way it never did on the Scottish mainland, used to accompany dances and sessions in a role elsewhere taken by the fiddle or accordion. The international bill, however, is only half the story. Viljandi is, at its core, an Estonian folk festival, and the home acts show why. The clearest demonstration is Puuluup, the duo of Ramo Teder and Marko Veisson, return to the festival where they arguably belong most. Their instrument is the talharpa, a four-stringed bowed lyre that had nearly disappeared from use by the late 19th century, now run through loopers and effect pedals to produce something both archaic and completely alive. They call it zombie-folk, and it has made them the most unlikely stars in Estonian music: a collaboration with hip-hop duo 5MIINUST that reached the Eurovision grand final in 2024, two US tours, an East Asia run through Japan, Hong Kong and Taiwan, and a feature-length documentary opening DocPoint Tallinn in February this year. Curly Strings work from a different angle, building arrangements in mandolin, fiddle, double bass and guitar around vocalist Eeva Talsi, drawing on bluegrass structure and Estonian song in equal measure, and Zetod arrive with 23 years of repertoire from Setomaa in southeastern Estonia, the same corner of the country that Kiiora call home, the trio performing century-old Seto dance tunes alongside Finno-Ugric material from neighbouring traditions. That question of what survives and how runs through the Estonian programme. OOPUS have spent two decades answering it one way: feeding bagpipes and archaic runic songs through analog acid synthesizers, movement-triggered lights and visuals, building one of the most distinctive live shows in Estonian music. Their third album Reivlender, out earlier this year, pushes that further, the title itself a compound of the Estonian word for “travel” and the English word for “rave”. Sounds and Stories from Ruhnu Island answer it another way entirely. Fiddlers Karoliina Kreintaal and Lee Taul and storyteller Kairi Leivo perform the traditional fiddle music of Ruhnu, a small Baltic island whose entire Swedish-speaking population fled to Sweden when Soviet forces arrived in 1944, taking the music with them. Their 2025 album Mere Mälu (“Echoes of the Sea“), built from archive recordings made on the island in 1938 and in Sweden after the exodus, won Authentic Folk Music of the Year at last year’s Estonian Folk Music Awards. Untsakad, the Viljandi ensemble formed in 1992, performed at the inaugural 1993 festival and return this year with Nõiduvad Huuled behind them, named Folk Album of the Year. Kuula Hetke, the duo of Kärt Pihlap and Katariina Tirmaste, took Debut Album of the Year at the same ceremony. They work with two flutes, voices and electronics, pulling apart folk melodies from the regions where each player’s family comes from and rebuilding them in the moment through improvisation. At this year’s festival they perform alongside visual artist Okeiko, who creates a live video backdrop in real time as the duo plays. One of the weekend’s most anticipated sets exists only because of this festival. Duo Ruut, Ann-Lisett Rebane and Katariina Kivi, have spent the past five years turning a single kannel into a full sonic argument: the two sit face to face across one instrument, four hands producing plucked lines, percussive rhythms and close harmonies, a setup that has taken them to Glastonbury, WOMEX, Roskilde and more than twenty countries, earned them Folk Album of the Month in The Guardian for their 2025 record Ilmateade, and made them Estonian Artist of the Year at last year’s folk music awards. For this festival only they expand into Duo Ruut³, joined by electric guitar, bass and percussion. Two projects that push the Baltic string tradition across the Estonian-Latvian border round out our look at the bill. Mari Kalkun, the Estonian singer, kannel player and composer whose album Stoonia Lood (Stories Of Stonia) came out on Peter Gabriel’s Real World Records in 2023 and has since been performed in twenty countries, meets Latvian kokle virtuoso Laima Jansone, whose work moves between meditative solo improvisation and rhythm-driven contemporary composition. The kannel and the kokle are cousins, box zithers that developed on either side of the Estonian-Latvian border from the same ancient instrument, whose playing traditions have been largely separate ever since. Tell Your Birds take that Baltic string tradition somewhere else entirely: Vija Moore on percussion, balafon and voice, Kärt Tambet on violin and voice, Kristīne Tukre on concert kokle, and Simone Spampinato on synthesizer and live electronics, setting the kokle‘s Baltic roots against West African balafon rhythms and electronic processing in the same room. Thirty-three years ago a generation that had spent decades being told what to sing built a festival to sing what they wanted. Some of the music on the bill this year would not exist if they hadn’t.   All the essentials, from programme to tickets and camping to glamping, can be found at viljandifolk.ee     The post Event Preview: Viljandi Folk Music Festival 2026 (Viljandi, Estonia; Thursday 23rd to Sunday 26th July 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Three drummers set up in Tayob J.‘s Lisbon studio and started playing something fairly ordinary. Then, as Tayob tells it, the rhythm started tasting of India and Africa, and he stopped, because now he knew what the track was about. He already had the name. A Mozambican friend had once told him to picture migration as geometry: most families draw a V, two starting points meeting in one person. His mother is Brazilian with Polish grandparents, his father Mozambican with roots in Goa. His family draws a W. That is the tenth track on A Beleza do Erro, his debut album, released 11 June on the independent label NOIZ DISCOS. After fifteen years engineering records for others at his Estúdio Noiz, it is the first with his own name on the cover. The drummers were Bateu Matou: Ivo Costa, Quim Albergaria and Rui “Riot” Pité, the latter two known from PAUS and Buraka Som Sistema. Costa and Pité have Goan roots of their own, which is partly why the rhythm drifted where it did. He brought in Selma Uamusse, the Mozambican singer long based in Portugal, to carry the hook, and Vinicius Terra, a rapper from Rio de Janeiro, for the verses. Under all of it he laid a heavy electronic sub-bass. He produced, recorded and mixed the track himself; Rodrigo Coimbra mastered it. items.body: This is the latest Reference Recordings release from Manfred Honeck and the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, and it is an excellent one: scrupulously prepared and played with great precision. In recent weeks I have listened to two Cleveland performances of Dvořák’s symphony (Szell on Sony Classical, Dohnányi on Decca), both recognized for their brilliant playing. Honeck and his players now match, and perhaps exceed, the ensemble unanimity and chamber-music sensitivity that distinguish those Cleveland albums. Neither of the older recordings offers engineering that equals the warmth, range, and transparency Reference achieves in Pittsburgh. New World Symphony Amazon Presto Apple In past reviews I have noted that Honeck’s interpretive ideas (unmarked dynamic tweaks, distinctive articulation and phrasing) occasionally cross into mannerism, and this new recording of the ‘New World Symphony’ has several examples. The most audible is an unmarked crescendo, not always but most often in the brass, applied to the second theme between the end of the antecedent phrase and the start of its consequent. On repeated listening I found it less distracting. Honeck also reshapes a crescendo (track 1, 2’17″) to make it more dramatic and, more radically, alters the timpani part around 2’33″, arguing in his notes that the timpani of Dvořák’s day could not do what he intended but modern instruments can. Finally, where many conductors pull back for the third theme (the flute solo at 6’45″), Honeck slams on the brakes, dropping to a substantially slower tempo for several measures before returning to speed. All these tweaks drew my attention from the music to the interpretation. Honeck’s reading of the slow movement takes its cue from the composer: “The second movement is a kind of Adagio, but one that differs from the classical form… it is in reality a study or sketch for a longer composition… after Longfellow’s Hiawatha.” It is beautiful: the opening and closing wind chorale has an organ-like sonority, and Ian Woodworth’s English horn solo is superb. The issue for me is that Honeck treats the music like a miniature tone poem, its dynamics and rhetorical gestures implying an unwritten program. That comes at the expense of any folk-like simplicity, and many hear this movement as a reflection of Native American and Black American melody. Bychkov (Czech Philharmonic, Pentatone) and Mackerras (Prague Symphony, Supraphon) take the plainer route, both a good deal faster, and I find their approach more convincing. Others will disagree. The last two movements are wholly successful, largely because there is less interpretive intervention and the orchestra is free to play with real artistry. Honeck and his players draw out a folksy warmth in the Scherzo’s Trio. Manfred Honeck. Photo © Felix Broede A few decades ago, critics sometimes wrote that Karajan’s Berlin recordings were too beautiful, so shaped and polished that they lost their humanness. I never understood the argument, yet here I feel something like it. I cannot fault the reading’s technical accomplishment, nor Honeck’s clear vision and his ability to realize it fully. What I miss is the vulnerability, the of-the-moment spontaneity that makes the recordings by Nelsons (Bavarian Radio Symphony, BR Klassik) and Stutzmann (Atlanta Symphony, Warner Classics) so moving. Carlos Simon’s Four Black American Dances makes a well-chosen coupling. Commissioned by the Boston Symphony Orchestra and Andris Nelsons, the work opens with the ecstatic Ring Shout, which lets the Pittsburgh players embrace their jazzier side. The Waltz is gently affecting, not least because Honeck draws a line to the sensuous writing of Strauss’s Der Rosenkavalier. The closing Holy Dance mimics a congregation speaking in tongues, building to a riotous Coda that levels off, unexpectedly, into a simple plagal cadence. Honeck and the orchestra bring the same attention and commitment here as in the symphony, and it is hard to imagine a better account. items.body: Turn my heart to stone Turn the sun away Feeling no desire Feeling no more pain The phrase “cold-hearted” usually lands as an accusation, a verdict passed on someone who has withheld affection or placed too much distance between themselves and the world. Yet emotional exhaustion can make that same coldness sound almost merciful. When every thought presses too hard, and every feeling remains exposed, numbness begins to resemble some sort of shelter: a private fantasy in which the heart can be hardened before anything else reaches it. Berlin post-punk quartet Agatha is Dead! enters that conflicted, icy state with “Cold-Hearted,” a collaboration with fellow Berlin artist SCHRAMM. The song’s accompanying video places both singers inside the crush of a darkened dance floor while the lyrics move between emotional exposure and the desire to feel nothing at all. The fourth and penultimate single taken from Agatha is Dead!’s forthcoming debut album, Concrete, due September 11 via Duchess Box Records, “Cold-Hearted” follows the disorientation of the previous single, “Strangers,” with a more physical and immediate form of unease. Deep bass moves beneath sheets of atmospheric synth before a cold, zigzagging gothic-rock guitar figure cuts across the arrangement. Its sharp repetition gives the song an instant hook, while the drums maintain a steady dance-floor pressure, quaking underneath. SCHRAMM takes the opening verse, delivering the words in a cool, velvety register that remains controlled even as the lyrics ask to be torn open and examined. The request is intimate and invasive at once: peel back the lies, expose what has been hidden, and keep the heart warm before it freezes beyond recovery. When Agatha is Dead!’s Lilly enters, her voice initially gathers beneath SCHRAMM’s before taking command of the chorus with “Turn my heart to stone” and “leave it all behind,” lines that launch the track into its dark dance groove. The second verse reverses the exchange. Lilly explains that she has already tried to open the other person and now fears that the same scrutiny will be turned upon her. Each singer recognizes a version of themselves in the other: guarded, capable of cruelty, and frightened by whatever might remain beneath their practiced distance. The chorus turns that mutual fear into a fantasy of emotional anesthesia, with stone offering protection at the cost of love, desire, and pain alike. Behind-the-scenes photo by Marvin Machler In the accompanying video, SCHRAMM first appears as a solitary figure in a white shirt and black tie, nearly reduced to silhouette by a fierce light at the rear of a crowded, fog-filled room. Dancers continually cross between the singer and the camera, concealing faces and breaking bodies into fragments. Close framing, motion blur, and ghosted double images make the room feel unstable, as though the party were being recalled through a memory already beginning to fail. As Lilly enters the song, the camera finds the two singers pressed together among the crowd. Their faces overlap in tight close-ups while hands, shoulders, and passing figures close around them. White backlight gradually gives way to deep blue, and the dancers’ movements grow less social than compulsive. The room offers physical contact everywhere, though little genuine comfort, turning the party into an apt setting for two people who want to be understood while recoiling from what such understanding might reveal. In the video’s final third, the crowd disappears, and Lilly stands alone beneath a narrow column of white light, her arms held behind her back and her white blouse creased tightly across her body. Her rigid posture gives the chorus’s transformation into stone a physical form. For several long moments, the movement that has filled the room is suspended, leaving her isolated in darkness as the refrain circles through its promises of emptiness. When the dance floor returns, it does so in a rush of blue and pale pink light. Lilly is absorbed once more into the surrounding bodies, singing and moving as the camera is jostled through the crowd. The release is temporary and deliberately ambiguous: the party provides motion, proximity, and escape, while the final backlit silhouettes leave the deeper question unresolved. The heart may survive by turning cold, but survival of that kind carries its own loneliness. Watch the video for “Cold-Hearted” below: Formed during the long winter of 2021, Agatha is Dead! began as a collaboration between Lilly and Noah, who developed their earliest songs in isolation before bringing them into the rehearsal room. Drawing from the emotional severity of Joy Division and the nocturnal romanticism of The Cure, the band balance melodic economy with mounting intensity. Joined by Joey Ramone Hansen on drums and Arthur on bass, the group soon established itself within Berlin’s live circuit. Since signing to Duchess Box Records in 2025, Agatha is Dead! have played a series of sold-out headline shows, including a Berlin appearance at Lido that reached capacity months in advance. In March 2026, the band traveled to the United States for SXSW, introducing their music to a wider international audience. That rapid ascent has established Agatha is Dead! as one of the most exciting new bands in the international post-punk scene and one of the finest groups Berlin has produced in more than a decade. Their selection for the Wunderkinder program at this year’s Reeperbahn Festival further confirms the growing attention surrounding them. SCHRAMM is the project of Berlin-based musician, photographer, and filmmaker Arne Schramm. Since releasing the debut EP I Made This for Myself (I Didn’t Make It for You) in 2022, SCHRAMM has developed a mixture of post-punk, new wave, and wiry UK indie rock, moving between German and English lyrics. The project’s latest EP, Something Smelling Funny, was released in February 2026. Agatha is Dead! will celebrate the release of Concrete with a special album-launch performance at Rough Trade Berlin on September 11. Further appearances at Reeperbahn Festival and Waves Vienna will lead into an October European tour, followed by another run of German dates in February 2027. Agatha is Dead! Tour Dates 2026 7 August — Bergfunk Open Air, Königs Wusterhausen 11 September — Rough Trade Berlin 13 September — BLOW Festival, Frankfurt 16 September — Reeperbahn Festival, Hamburg 1–3 October — Waves Festival, Vienna 8 October — Café Glocksee, Hannover 9 October — Naumanns Tanzlokal, Leipzig 10 October — Nürnberg Pop at Club Stereo 11 October — Engelsburg, Erfurt 13 October — Bumann & Sohn, Cologne 14 October — Schon Schön, Mainz 15 October — Substanz, Munich 16 October — B72, Vienna Agatha is Dead! items.body: Just a couple more days ’til the Senior Staff are (briefly) aloft and flying to Calgary for Terminus. As we’ve been gassing on about on the podcast it’s an absolutely stacked lineup with faves new and old, but as always a huge part of the anticipation for Terminus comes via the incredible community of friends and festival fam we’ve all built together over the years. Looking forward to seeing y’all, and as always, if this is your first time at the fest come and tap one of us on the shoulder – first round’s on us. FRACTIONS ARE HIDING AMONGST US ACTORS, “Youth” One more advance single before Vancouver’s mighty ACTORS drop their third album. Unlike the bass-led and somewhat tense “CTRL” and “Left On Read”, “Youth” taps into the band’s sweet, dreamy side, with a nice laid back verse and some fun layered vocal punch-ins before a suprisingly big wash of shoegaze guitars sweeps through the mix, capped by a synth arp climax that feels just right. Youth by ACTORS Damage Control x OHMElectronic, “Manifesto” A collaboration between OHMElectronic and the already collaborative intercontinental Damage Control project, there’s a nice mix of influences and styles in this new single, despite its restraint. Bass and percussion programming spatter and blur into one another while the icier pads maintain their own movement, seemingly in a separate region of the stratosphere. Manifesto by Damage Control x OHMElectronic Vacios Cuerpos, “CIELO = INFIERNO” A great slice of classic atmospheric post-punk from Mexican act Vacios Cuerpos, who specialize in that field. A big part of it is in how the standard musical elements of the style – twangy guitars, low vocals, programmed drums and heaps of reverb – all sit so nicely alongside each other, really allowing the track’s melody to breathe. CIELO = INFIERNO by Vacíos Cuerpos Filmmaker, “Breaking The Grid” Regular readers know the drill by now: you can’t hope to stay wholly abreast of the constant torrent of Filmmaker releases, you just dip in and out when you can. The lead cut from new LP Externalism (the third one to see release this year thus far) brings in some classic downtempo cinematics alongside Faunes Efe’s trademark lo-fi electro/EBM hybrid style, and the result almost feels like Haujobb griming it up. Externalism by Filmmaker FRACTIONS, “Love Like Ice” Czech duo FRACTIONS have really been stretching their wings of late; while originally lumped in with the broader techno-ebm movement, their last EP Post-Club had them taking on a more high-bpm, song-based approach. New single “Love Like Ice” continues with that, applying their combined production skills to a fast-moving electropop number with a big guitar finale we didn’t hear coming but worked perfectly. Not even sure what to call what the band is doing now genre-wise, but it sure is hitting the spot. Love Like Ice by FRACTIONS Virulents & Grauhaus, “Screamsheets” Lastly, a little bit of lithe dark techno from LA which dabbles a little bit in a cyber direction that draws from early 2010’s industrial clubs as much as modern techno. Of note for longtime heads? One of your producers behind the Austere EP, Grauhaus, is none other than one-third of long, long, LONG time faves of the Senior Staff, NCC. items.body: Band: Le Grand Sbam | Album: Janus | Genre: Zeuhl, Avant-prog | Year: 2026 From: Lyon, France | Label: Dur et Doux For fans of: Magma, PoiL, Frank Zappa Bandcamp Le Grand Sbam is a band I’ve been aware of since their founding. I’ve listened to their previous two albums, but neither one really quite clicked with me. I could tell there were a lot of elements I liked. This is a band I should like, but it just didn’t quite coalesce. I went into Janus, their third full-length release, with my usual hopefulness for a good experience. There have been no major changes to their sound, but something just hit a bit different this time, and I wound up really enjoying it. This work is apparently an excerpt of a “Chthulu opera”–also titled Janus–written by Antoine Arnera, keyboardist for both this band and PoiL. It flows together as one massive, unified piece, and it shows incredible vision and ambition. This opera–about environmentalism, feminism, and flatulence–is paired with music that is simultaneously serious, complex, and whimsical. After a brief, sound-effect-laden intro (there are seven more brief interludes on this record which I will not be covering), the album kicks off in earnest with “Ouverture”. Ritualistic chanting, thumping drums, plinking harp, and an array of wind and reed instruments swirl in an otherworldly melange. Modern classical, experimental rock, and influences from beyond Western musical traditions fold and twist in on each other in ways that feel coherently experimental. “Tourbifouette II” opens with tense piano and pizzicato strings beneath rich, multilayered vocal arrangements. Slowly, the music grows in intensity, as if it’s fighting against the restrained opening moments. There are moments where the full orchestra assembled for this record bursts through with manic fury, but that underlying tension always resurfaces. Hip-hop and electronica immediately smack the listener in the face on “Ragga II”. The electronics are wonky, and the string and wind instruments often provide dramatic stabs of contrast. While I appreciate the bold nature of this experiment, I am glad it’s the second-shortest proper song on the record. Despite being under three minutes, it begins to wear a bit thin by the end of its runtime. “Mécanique des pompes” opens quietly, giving a floating, dreamlike feel. The many different layers of the vocals add to both the depth and ethereal nature of this piece. Occasional harsh blasts of synth show that this idyll could burst at any moment. This track flows immediately into “Hypnose I” with no short interlude. The rhythm is irregular and disorienting, as if the music is trying to stand up but cannot find its footing. This staggering feel does go on for longer than is needed, but the band eventually shifts into a new gear. Vocals, drums, and strings provide a dramatic, rolling soundscape. “Duopode II” features some exciting, tangled guitar lines that sound like Discipline-era King Crimson being played by Frank Zappa. Clarinet and bassoon add dramatic texture, and some of the vocal lines have a nearly-Caribbean feel to them.  Energetic piano, evoking a chase, opens up “Tourbiflouette I”. Things are taut and restrained, with guitar anxiously plinking along as the drums tirelessly propel the track along. This song is a slow build, but it doesn’t feel drawn-out. There’s a sense of slowly-growing doom, and the wild, ranted vocals only add to that feeling. “Ragga I” dips back into some hip-hop flavors, but the backing is more firmly rooted in avant-garde classical and rock music. This brings us to the longest song on the album: “Symbiotshish II”. From the get-go, the mood is frenetic and frantic. Speedy, technical piano lines drive things forward, but strings and reeds offer a lush backing. This piece vacillates between classic dark avant-prog and passages that would feel at home in a horror film score, but it all makes sense, somehow. The vocal arrangements here are particularly complex, full of mellifluous singing, mantric chanting, frenzied trilling, and oddball yelping. It all ties together in the finale, offering a glorious conclusion. This operatic excerpt ends with “Epilogue”, a slow and somewhat mournful classical composition. Janus is a lot to take in. The music is dense as hell, and I can see it’s taken Le Grand Sbam six years to put this record out. There are so many individual elements that all coalesce quite well. This isn’t a perfect record, mind you. A couple songs do drag at moments, and the interludes don’t really do much. But on the whole, this is both a thrilling and challenging listen that has a lot to offer on repeated plays. Score: 85/100

If I can't go a day without my metal fix, I don't want to know what'll happen to my mental health. Traditional Addict
items.body: Marijuana, alcohol, gambling—these are Traditional Addictions. I've remained abstinent from these three; music is my addiction, corny as it may be. If I can't go a day without my metal fix, I don't want to know what'll happen to my mental health. Canada's Yeti On Horseback go much darker on their second LP, however, bringing forth another record of drawn-out atmospheres and crushing environments In a mixture of sludge, doom, and everything drab. Traditional Addictions isn't a "celebration of life"; it's a pained spit to the grave of the subject at a pitiful, minimalistic gathering. The album's opener, "Drug Addict," is a blunt offering that spans thirteen minutes and isn't even the lengthiest track. I can't safely tell whether it's romanticizing or looking down upon the addict in question. By the screams, the rapid breathing, the repetitiveness of the plodding tempo, the ending feedback and detailing of the habitual spiraling consequences of addiction, I'm inclined to say it's negative.Note: The video for "Drug Addict" starts with ELEVEN MINUTES of extra sampling and whatever. The album version pertains to the regular fourteen.Closer "Erotic Goth Dad" may have a seemingly out-of-place name, but it's the heaviest and most expansive piece, constituting the band's self-proclaimed opus. While it played out, I took a closer inspection at the album artwork: Conjoined twins, a lobster, a mortar and pestle, a seahorse, and a patient with a severe tumor are just some of the items plastered around the band name and album title. If they all have something in common, it's completely cryptic, and the answer isn't found in the fourteen minutes of crescendoing, psychedelic metal in the closing track, either. It's a trip all in its own, and obdurate in its harshness and solidity, with post-metal shining delicately in the song's waning minutes.Only two, nine-minute songs bridge the gap between "Drug Addict" and "Erotic Goth Dad". On these tracks, Yeti On Horseback proves to be clever with atmospheric play, with "Through With This Flesh" supplying enough to cover the opener two times over. Vocalists "R.P." and "S.M." experiment with layered vocals, which are most prominent in this track. Blackened metal snarls fight with strained wails, achieving more than a song 1.4-times longer. "Mariner's Lament" is the weaker link between the two, relying more laboriously on ambience than upfront brutality. Nevertheless, these two cuts are greatly welcomed among, as the forty-seven-minute-long runtime probablywouldn't be as palatable as a two-song recording.In spite of its title, Traditional Addictions is hard to immediately acclimate to. It isn't the most accessible doom-laced metal up for listening, and it may take a while for the looping, chunky start to envelop you, but Traditional Addictions is a drug in doom metal form, with each sustained guitar strum just another needle on the curb. Traditional Addictions by Yeti On Horseback
